The branching fraction (ignoring tiny CP‑violating effects) can be written compactly as \[ \boxed{ \mathcal B(B_q\!\to\!\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) = \frac{G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}} |V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}|^{2} f_{B_q}^{2} M_{B_q}\tau_{B_q}\, \sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^{2}}{M_{B_q}^{2}}} \Bigl[ |P|^{2} + \Bigl(1-\frac{4m_\mu^{2}}{M_{B_q}^{2}}\Bigr) |S|^{2} \Bigr], } \] with \[ \begin{aligned} P &\equiv C_{10}^{\rm eff} + \frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}} (C_{P} - C_{P}^{\prime}),\\ S &\equiv \frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}} (C_{S} - C_{S}^{\prime}), \end{aligned} \qquad C_{10}^{\rm eff}=C_{10}^{\rm SM}+C_{10}^{\rm NP}. \] Thus **any non‑zero scalar/pseudoscalar contribution \(S\) or a sizable modification of \(P\) directly changes the rate**. --- ## 3. What the experiments have measured (as of 2024) | Observable | LHCb + CMS (Run‑1 + Run‑2) | ATLAS (Run‑2) | World average | |---|---|---|---| | \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) | \((3.09 \pm 0.46_{\rm stat} \pm 0.15_{\rm syst})\times10^{-9}\) | \((3.0^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\pm0.3)\times10^{-9}\) | \((3.10 \pm 0.37)\times10^{-9}\) | | \(\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) | \((1.01^{+0.51}_{-0.33})\times10^{-10}\) | — | \((1.0^{+0.5}_{-0.3})\times10^{-10}\) | | Effective lifetime \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) (for \(B_s\)) | \(1.70 \pm 0.13\) ps (consistent with SM 1.61 ps) | — | — | | Ratio \(R_{\mu\mu}= \mathcal B(B_d)/\mathcal B(B_s)\) | \(0.032 \pm 0.018\) | — | — | *The uncertainties are now dominated by statistics; systematic errors (especially lattice inputs for \(f_{B_q}\)) are at the 2 % level.* **Key point:** The measured \(B_{s}\) rate is **within 1σ** of the SM prediction, while the \(B_{d}\) rate is compatible but still statistically limited. Any BSM model must therefore reproduce \[ \frac{\mathcal B_{\rm exp}}{\mathcal B_{\rm SM}} = 0.85\!-\!1.15\quad (95\%~\text{CL}) \] for \(B_s\) and a similar ball‑park for \(B_d\) once the error shrinks. --- ## 4. How the measurement translates into limits on Wilson coefficients Assuming NP contributes *only* to one coefficient at a time, one can solve the above branching‑ratio expression for the allowed range: | Coefficient | 95 % CL bound (real) | |---|---| | \(\Delta C_{10}=C_{10}^{\rm NP}\) | \(-0.34 < \Delta C_{10} < 0.12\) | | \(\Delta C_{10}^{\prime}\) | \(-0.31 < \Delta C_{10}^{\prime} < 0.31\) | | \(\mathrm{Re}\,(C_{P}-C_{P}^{\prime})\) | \(-0.05 < \frac{M_{B_s}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}}(C_{P}-C_{P}^{\prime}) < 0.04\) | | \(\mathrm{Re}\,(C_{S}-C_{S}^{\prime})\) | \(|\frac{M_{B_s}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}}(C_{S}-C_{S}^{\prime})| < 0.03\) | | Complex phases: \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.3\) and \(|C_{P,S}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.05\) (roughly) | | *These numbers come from the “single‑operator” fits performed by the *UTfit* and *Flavour Lattice Averaging Group* (FLAG) groups, see e.g. [UTfit 2023] and [EOS 2024].* If several operators are present simultaneously, the constraints are correlated; global fits in the \((C_{10},C_{10}^{\prime},C_{P},C_{S})\) space show elongated allowed ellipses, but the **overall magnitude of any NP contribution cannot exceed about 30 % of the SM amplitude**. --- ## 5. Implications for specific classes of BSM models Below is a non‑exhaustive “rule‑book” of what the current \(B_{q}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) data **exclude or severely constrain**. | Model / Feature | Typical contribution to the effective operators | Why it is constrained (or still viable) | |---|---|---| | **Minimal Supersymmetric SM (MSSM) at large \(\tan\beta\)** | Enhances scalar/pseudoscalar operators via Higgs‑mediated penguins: \(\displaystyle C_{S,P}\propto \frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{M_{A}^{2}}\). | The measured rate forces \(\displaystyle \frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{M_{A}^{2}} \lesssim 10^{-3}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\).
*Result*: For \(\tan\beta\sim 50\) one needs \(M_{A}\gtrsim 1.5\) TeV. Low‑mass \(A\) bosons with \(\tan\beta>30\) are **ruled out**. | | **Generic Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Models (2HDM‑I,II, X, Y)** | Same Higgs‑mediated scalar/pseudoscalar pattern, but with model‑dependent Yukawa factors. | The *type‑II* (SUSY‑like) case is essentially forced into the **decoupling regime** (heavy extra Higgs \(\gtrsim 1\) TeV) unless \(\tan\beta\) is tiny. Type‑X models with leptophilic Higgs can survive if the lepton Yukawa coupling is small. | | **Leptoquarks (LQ)** | Tree‑level exchange generates vector operators (shifts in \(C_{9,10}^{(\prime)}\)) and, for scalar LQs, also scalar/pseudoscalar pieces. | To affect \(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) anomalies, a LQ with mass \(\sim\) 1 TeV and coupling \(g\sim0.3\) is typical. The same coupling contributes to \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) at **order \(g^{2}/M_{\rm LQ}^{2}\)**, leading to \(|\Delta C_{10}|\sim0.1\). The current bound permits such a LQ *provided* it does not also generate large scalar operators (i.e. it must be a **vector LQ** such as \(U_{1}\) with left‑handed couplings). | | **Z′ bosons with flavour‑changing \(b\!-\!s\) couplings** | Modifies \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) (and possibly \(C_{9}^{(\prime)}\)) via tree‑level exchange: \(\Delta C_{10}\propto \frac{g_{bs}^{L,R}g_{\mu\mu}^{A}}{M_{Z'}^{2}}\). | The constraint \(|\Delta C_{10}|\lesssim0.3\) translates into \(\frac{|g_{bs}^{L,R} g_{\mu\mu}^{A}|}{M_{Z'}^{2}} \lesssim 1.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{TeV}^{-2}\).
*Consequence*: For a weak‑scale \(Z′\) (1 TeV) the product of couplings must be ≲ 0.04, i.e. **highly suppressed** flavour‑changing coupling or a mostly axial muon coupling. Many “simplified” \(Z′\) models proposed to explain the \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) anomalies are still viable but now sit near the edge of the allowed region. | | **Models with Light (MeV‑GeV) Axion‑like particles (ALPs)** | Can induce effective pseudoscalar operator \(C_{P}\) via mixing with the Higgs or via derivative couplings to quarks. | The bound \(|C_{P}|\lesssim 5\times10^{-3}\) translates to an **effective scale** \(\Lambda_{\rm ALP}\gtrsim 10\) TeV for order‑one ALP–muon coupling, ruling out the *very* light‑ALP explanation of the muon‑\(g-2\) anomaly unless the ALP couples **predominantly** to photons (not to quarks). | | **Composite Higgs / Partial compositeness** | Generates flavor‑non‑universal shifts in \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) through heavy vector resonances. | The data force the compositeness scale \(f\) to be **\(> 2\) TeV** for typical anarchic couplings, tightening earlier electroweak‑precision bounds. | | **Extra dimensions (e.g. RS models with bulk fermions)** | KK‑gluon or Z′‑like excitations modify \(C_{10}\) and can also produce scalar currents if Higgs is localized. | To keep \(|\Delta C_{10}|<0.3\) one needs KK masses **\(M_{\rm KK}\gtrsim 5\) TeV**, a limit comparable to direct LHC searches. | | **Flavor‑violating Higgs couplings** (e.g. \(h\to bs\)) | Generates scalar operators at one‑loop, proportional to the product \(y_{bs}\,y_{\mu\mu}\). | Current limits on \(\mathcal B(B_s\to\mu\mu)\) imply \(|y_{bs}| \lesssim 10^{-3}\) (for SM‑like muon Yukawa), essentially **excluding observable \(h\to bs\) branching fractions** (> \(10^{-5}\)). | ### Visual summary (allowed region) A typical global fit in the \((\Delta C_{10}, C_{P})\) plane (all other coefficients set to zero) looks like this: ``` C_P ^ | .------ 95% CL ellipse ------. | / \ | | SM point (0,0) | | \ / | '---------------------------' +------------------------------------> ΔC10 ``` The ellipse’s semi‑axes are roughly 0.3 (horizontal) and 0.04 (vertical), reflecting the much tighter bound on pseudoscalar contributions. --- ## 6. Complementarity with other observables | Observable | Sensitivity | How it helps disentangle NP | |---|---|---| | **\(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) angular observables** (e.g. \(P_5'\)) | Probes \(C_{9}^{(\prime)}\) and \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) (vector operators). | If a model shifts only \(C_{10}\), the pattern in \(B_s\to\mu\mu\) + angular data points to axial‑vector NP. | | **\(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\)** | Purely left‑handed operator \(O_{L}\). | Correlates with \(C_{10}\) shifts in many \(Z'\) models; combined limits can pin down the chiral structure. | | **\(B_{s}\) mixing (\(\Delta M_s\))** | Sensitive to the same flavour‑changing coupling that appears in tree‑level \(Z'\) exchange. | Strong constraints on the product \(g_{bs}^{L}g_{bs}^{R}\). | | **\(B\to\ell\nu\) and \(B\to D^{(*)}\tau\nu\)** | Test charged‑current scalar operators. | In 2HDM, the same \(\tan\beta/M_A\) that affects \(B_s\to\mu\mu\) also modifies these decays; the combined picture rules out low \(\tan\beta\)–high \(\tan\beta\) corners. | | **Muon \(g-2\)** | Requires new light states coupling to muons. | If those states also couple to quarks they would appear in \(B_s\to\mu\mu\); the non‑observation restricts many explanations. | Thus **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is the cornerstone** of a broader flavour‑physics network that collectively chips away at BSM parameter space. --- ## 7. Future prospects and the next “door” to discovery | Milestone | Anticipated precision | Impact on NP | |---|---|---| | **Run‑3 & Run‑4 LHCb (2025‑2029)** | \(\sim 5\%\) total uncertainty on \(B_s\to\mu\mu\); first observation of the **effective lifetime** with < 5 % precision. | Lifetime probes the *CP‑odd* vs *CP‑even* admixture, i.e. the relative size of scalar vs axial contributions. A deviation at the 10 % level would signal NP even if the branching ratio is SM‑like. | | **High‑Luminosity LHC (HL‑LHC) ATLAS/CMS** | \(\sim 3\%\) (combined) on \(B_s\) rate, first \(B_d\) observation with \(\sim30\%\) error. | Tightens \(|\Delta C_{10}|\) to \(\lesssim 0.1\); pushes scalar bounds below the 1 % level. | | **Belle II (full dataset ~50 ab\(^{-1}\))** | Not competitive for \(B_s\) but will improve **\(B_d\to\mu\mu\)** to ~\(20\%\). | Provides an independent cross‑check and a clean environment for CP‑asymmetry studies. | | **Lattice QCD** | Decay constants \(f_{B_{s,d}}\) known to \(\sim0.5\%\). | Systematic theory error becomes sub‑percent, so experimental improvements dominate the constraint. | | **Global EFT fits (flavio, EOS, HEPfit…)** | Include all \(b\to s\ell\ell\) data, with correlated theory errors. | Will be able to **resolve degeneracies** between \(C_{10}\) and scalar coefficients, especially once the lifetime measurement is precise. | If the central values remain exactly at the SM predictions, the **95 % CL upper limits** on the absolute values of NP Wilson coefficients will shrink roughly as \[ |C_{10}^{\rm NP}| \lesssim 0.07,\qquad |C_{S,P}| \lesssim 0.015, \] effectively **closing the “large‑\(\tan\beta\) Higgs” window** and forcing any viable BSM model to be either (i) *high‑scale* (≥ 10 TeV) or (ii) *highly flavour‑aligned* (SM‑like couplings). Conversely, any small but statistically significant tension (say a 2–3 σ excess in the rate or a lifetime shift) would immediately point to one of the operator structures above and provide a very sharp target for model builders. --- ## 8. Take‑away for a theorist or experimentalist 1. **Precision → power**: Because the SM prediction is clean, a 10 % measurement already translates into an \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})\) bound on the effective NP scale for *tree‑level* mediators. 2. **Operator‐by‐operator limits**: Scalars/pseudoscalars are the most tightly constrained; vector/axial‑vector shifts are limited at the 20‑30 % level of the SM amplitude. 3. **Model‑building rule‑book**: *Discard* low‑mass (≲ 1 TeV) heavy‑Higgs sectors with large \(\tan\beta\); *allow* Z′/LQ models only if the flavour‑changing coupling product is ≤ 0.04 (1 TeV/ \(M_{Z'}\))²; *require* compositeness scales > 2–3 TeV. 4. **Complementary observables** (angular analyses, \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\), mixing) are essential to pin down the chiral/CP structure. 5. **Future data will either** (a) push the allowed NP scale to > 10 TeV (making indirect flavour constraints competitive with direct LHC searches) **or** (b) reveal a subtle deviation that will single out a specific operator, dramatically narrowing the landscape of viable BSM theories. In short, **precise measurements of the ultra‑rare decays \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) are now the most stringent “filter” on almost any extension of the Standard Model that introduces new sources of flavour violation or new scalar/pseudoscalar interactions**. The coming decade of LHCb, ATLAS, CMS, and Belle II results will either seal the SM’s verdict or open a narrow doorway to new physics.

question: What practical steps and diagnostics should I use to choose, estimate, and validate a single-variate stochastic process for a financial time series that exhibits both fat tails and mean-reversion?
model_answer:
Below is a **road‑map you can follow step‑by‑step** to pick, estimate, and validate a **single‑variate stochastic model** for a financial series that (i) shows **mean‑reversion** and (ii) displays **fat‑tailed / non‑Gaussian** increments. The guide is organized into four major blocks: 1. **Exploratory diagnostics – does the data really need both features?** 2. **Model class shortlist – candidates that can generate mean‑reversion *and* heavy tails.** 3. **Parameter estimation – practical, robust methods for each candidate.** 4. **Model validation & selection – statistical tests, out‑of‑sample checks, and “stress‑test” diagnostics.** At the end you’ll find a **quick‑reference checklist** and a few **R / Python code snippets** you can drop into a notebook. --- ## 1. Exploratory Diagnostics | Goal | Test / Plot | Interpretation | |------|------------|----------------| | **Mean‑reversion** | • **Autocorrelation function (ACF)** of level and of first differences
• **Partial ACF** (PACF)
• **Variance‑ratio test** (Lo & MacKinlay)
• **Hurst exponent** (R/S, DFA) | A rapid exponential decay of the ACF (or a strong negative lag‑1 PACF) is a classic OU signature. Hurst < 0.5 also points to mean‑reversion. | | **Fat tails / excess kurtosis** | • **Histogram + fitted normal**
• **Q‑Q plot** against Normal and against a heavy‑tail reference (e.g., Student‑t)
• **Sample kurtosis** (excess > 3)
• **Tail index** (Hill estimator, Pickands, QQ‑estimator)
• **Time‑scaled kurtosis** (check if kurtosis shrinks as √Δ t) | Heavy‑tailed if kurtosis ≫ 3, tail‑index ξ ∈ (0, 4) (or tail exponent α < 4). | | **Stationarity of moments** | • **ADF / KPSS tests** on the level & on the squared series
• **Engle’s ARCH LM test** (to spot conditional heteroskedasticity) | Mean‑reversion usually implies level stationary; heavy tails may come from jumps or stochastic volatility, so check for ARCH effects. | | **Jump / discontinuity detection** | • **BNS jump‑test** (Bollerslev–Tauchen)
• **Bipower variation vs. realized variance** (Barndorff‑Nielsen & Shephard)
• **Cumulative sum (CUSUM) of standardized residuals** | If jumps are present, you’ll need a jump component (e.g., OU‑jump, Lévy OU). | | **Distribution of increments at several horizons** | • Compute returns ΔX_t(Δ) for Δ = 1, 5, 20, 60 minutes (or daily, weekly)
• Plot kurtosis vs. Δ on log‑log scale
• Fit stable law or tempered‑stable law | Heavy tails that **persist** across horizons point to a Lévy‐type driver; tails that fade faster suggest a *finite‑variance* jump/mixture model. | **Practical tip:** If the ACF decays roughly as \(e^{-\kappa t}\) and the marginal distribution is clearly non‑Gaussian, you have the right ingredients for a **mean‑reverting Lévy (or jump‑diffusion) Ornstein‑Uhlenbeck** process. --- ## 2. Model Class Shortlist | Model | Dynamics | How it captures the two features | |-------|----------|-----------------------------------| | **OU‑diffusion (Gaussian OU)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + \sigma dW_t\) | Mean‑reversion via κ; no fat tails (Gaussian). Use only as a baseline. | | **OU‑with‑jumps (Merton‑type OU)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + \sigma dW_t + dJ_t\)
\(J_t\) = compound Poisson with jump size distribution (e.g., Normal, double‑exponential) | Mean‑reversion + occasional large moves → heavier tails (finite variance). | | **Lévy‑OU (OU driven by a pure‑jump Lévy process)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + dL_t\)
\(L_t\) = α‑stable, tempered‑stable, Variance‑Gamma, CGMY, NIG, etc. | Mean‑reversion + infinite‑activity jumps → power‑law tails. | | **OU with Stochastic Volatility (SV‑OU)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + \sqrt{V_t}\, dW_t\)
\(dV_t = a(b-V_t)dt + \eta\sqrt{V_t}\,dZ_t\) (e.g., CIR) | Mean‑reversion in level; heavy tails arise from volatility clustering. | | **Mean‑Reverting GARCH (MR‑GARCH)** | \(X_t = \mu + \phi (X_{t-1}-\mu) + \epsilon_t\)
\(\epsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t,\; \sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \epsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\) | Discrete‑time analogue; fat tails from conditional heteroskedasticity. | | **Hybrid (OU + SV + Jumps)** | Combine the OU drift with both stochastic volatility and a jump‐component. | Most flexible – often over‑parameterised for a *single* series, but useful for robustness checks. | **When to pick which?** | Situation | Recommended model | |-----------|-------------------| | **Tail index ≈ 2–3, persistent power‑law tails** | **Lévy‑OU** (α‑stable or tempered‑stable driver). | | **Tail index > 3, occasional outliers, clear jump dates** | **OU‑with‑jumps** (compound Poisson). | | **Strong ARCH effects, volatility clustering** | **OU‑SV** (or MR‑GARCH). | | **Both heavy tails *and* clustering** | **Hybrid OU‑SV‑Jumps** (or a *tempered stable* OU which can mimic both). | --- ## 3. Parameter Estimation Below are practical, implementation‑ready techniques for the most used candidates. ### 3.1 Gaussian OU (benchmark) | Method | Description | Code tip | |--------|------------|----------| | **Maximum Likelihood (Exact)** | Transition density is normal: \(X_{t+\Delta}|X_t \sim \mathcal N\big(\mu + e^{-\kappa\Delta}(X_t-\mu),\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}(1-e^{-2\kappa\Delta})\big)\). | In R: `ou <- sde::OUfit(x, dt)`; in Python: `statsmodels.tsa.statespace.structural.UnobservedComponents` with a mean‑reverting component. | | **OLS on discretised form** | Regress \(X_{t+\Delta}\) on \(X_t\). | Good initial guess for κ. | ### 3.2 OU‑with‑jumps (Merton‑type) | Method | Description | Implementation | |--------|-------------|----------------| | **Exact MLE via EM algorithm** | E‑step: compute expected number and sizes of jumps given current parameters (using Kalman filter for the continuous part). M‑step: update κ, σ, jump intensity λ, jump‑size parameters (μ_J, σ_J). | R: `yuima::setModel` with `jump = list(type = "compoundPoisson")`; Python: custom EM (see *github.com/akram-ali/OUJumpEM*). | | **Generalised Method of Moments (GMM)** | Use moments of increments: mean, variance, third/fourth moments; write them as functions of parameters. | `gmm` package (R) or `linearmodels` (Python). | | **Characteristic‑function (CF) matching** | Fit parameters by minimizing distance between empirical CF of increments and the analytical CF of OU‑jump model. | `cffit` (R) or `statsmodels`’ `fit_cf`. | ### 3.3 Lévy‑OU The **exact transition density** is rarely closed‑form, but the **characteristic function** is known: \[ \phi_{X_{t+\Delta}|X_t}(u)=\exp\!\Big\{ iu e^{-\kappa\Delta}X_t + iu\mu(1-e^{-\kappa\Delta}) + \int_{0}^{\Delta}\!\psi\big(u e^{-\kappa(\Delta-s)}\big)ds \Big\}, \] where \(\psi(u)\) is the Lévy exponent of the driving Lévy process \(L_t\). | Method | Steps | Practical notes | |--------|-------|-----------------| | **CF‑based MLE (Fourier inversion)** | 1. Write log‑likelihood using the analytic CF.
2. Numerically invert (FFT) to obtain the density at each observation.
3. Optimise. | Use `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.cftool` or `scipy.fft`. Works well for **CGMY**, **NIG**, **Tempered Stable** where \(\psi(u)\) is simple. | | **GMM with empirical characteristic function** | Minimise \(\sum_{i}| \hat\phi(u_i)-\phi(u_i;\theta) |^2 w_i\). Choose a grid of u’s (e.g., 0.5,1,1.5). | Very fast, robust to miss‑specification of diffusion part. | | **Indirect Inference (Simulated Method of Moments)** | Simulate many paths for a trial θ, compute moments (e.g., autocovariance, kurtosis) and match to data. | Good when the Lévy driver has **infinite variance** (α‑stable). Use `PyLevy` or `levy` R package for simulation. | | **Bayesian inference (MCMC)** | Use a particle filter for the latent OU state, embed in a Metropolis‑Hastings scheme for θ. | Packages: `pymc` (Python) + `theano.tensor.nnet` for Lévy exponent; `rstan` with custom likelihood. | ### 3.4 OU‑with Stochastic Volatility (OU‑SV) | Method | Steps | |--------|-------| | **Quasi‑Maximum Likelihood (QML)** – treat the model as a **state‑space** system: level X_t is observed, variance V_t is latent. Apply an **Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)** or **Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)** to compute the likelihood. | Python `filterpy` or R `KFAS`. | | **Particle MCMC** – bootstrap particle filter for V_t, then PMMH for parameters. | `pymc3` + `particles` library, or `nimble` in R. | | **Two‑step GMM** – first estimate κ, μ by OLS on the level; next estimate SV parameters from squared residuals using standard SV GMM. | Quick diagnostic; good for initial values. | ### 3.5 Discrete‑time MR‑GARCH | Method | Description | |--------|-------------| | **Standard MLE** (t‑distribution innovations) | `rugarch` (R) or `arch` (Python) with `model='GARCH', dist='t'`. | | **Penalised likelihood** (to avoid over‑fitting κ against GARCH α,β) | Add L2 penalty on κ. | --- ## 4. Model Validation & Selection ### 4.1 In‑sample goodness‑of‑fit | Diagnostic | How to compute | What to look for | |------------|----------------|------------------| | **Standardised residuals** \( \hat\varepsilon_t = (X_t-\hat\mu_t)/\hat\sigma_t\) | For diffusion‑only models: use analytical conditional variance. For jump/Lévy models: compute *conditional* variance via the model (e.g., using the Lévy variance if finite; otherwise use *truncated* variance). | Residuals should be i.i.d. N(0,1) **or** i.i.d. t‑distributed with the chosen df. | | **Ljung‑Box test on residuals & squared residuals** | `Box.test(resid, lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box")` | No remaining autocorrelation or ARCH‑type dependence. | | **Empirical vs. model CF** | Plot \(|\hat\phi(u) - \phi(u;\hat\theta)|\) over a grid of u. | Small uniform distance (≤ 0.02) indicates good fit. | | **Tail‑fit test** | Compare empirical tail index (Hill) with that implied by the fitted Lévy exponent (e.g., α for α‑stable, tail parameter for CGMY). | Difference < 0.1 is acceptable. | | **Kolmogorov‑Smirnov / Anderson‑Darling** on **one‑step ahead predictive distribution** | Simulate predictive CDF using the fitted model, run KS test vs. observed next‑step value. | p‑value > 0.05 suggests no evidence against model. | ### 4.2 Out‑of‑sample performance | Procedure | Steps | |-----------|-------| | **Rolling‑window forecast** | 1. Fit model on window (e.g., 500 obs). 2. Produce 1‑step‑ahead density forecast (Monte‑Carlo or analytic). 3. Move window forward and repeat. | | **Scoring rules** | Compute **Log‑Score** (average log‑likelihood of out‑of‑sample observations), **Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS)**, and **Quantile Score** at high quantiles (95%, 99%). | | **Value‑at‑Risk (VaR) back‑test** | Use the predictive distribution to generate VaR(95%) and VaR(99%). Load data # ------------------------------------------------- price = pd.read_csv('data.csv', parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date')['close'] ret = np.log(price).diff().dropna().values # log‑returns, assumed stationary # ------------------------------------------------- # 2. CF‑GMM for tempered stable OU (CGMY driver) # ------------------------------------------------- # Lévy exponent of CGMY (tempered stable) def psi_cgmy(u, C=1.0, G=5.0, M=5.0, Y=0.5): # ψ(u) = C * Γ(-Y) * [(M - iu)^Y - M^Y + (G + iu)^Y - G^Y] from mpmath import gamma return C * gamma(-Y) * ((M - 1j*u)**Y - M**Y + (G + 1j*u)**Y - G**Y) def cf_ou_jump(u, theta, dt): """Characteristic function of OU driven by Lévy (CGMY).""" kappa, mu, C, G, M, Y = theta exp_term = 1j * u * (mu * (1 - np.exp(-kappa*dt))) int_psi = 0.0 # analytical integral of ψ over [0,dt] via quadrature from mpmath import quad int_psi = quad(lambda s: psi_cgmy(u*np.exp(-kappa*(dt-s)), C, G, M, Y), [0, dt]) return np.exp(exp_term + int_psi) def gmm_obj(theta, data, dt, u_grid, w): # empirical CF emp_cf = np.mean(np.exp(1j*u_grid[:,None]*data), axis=1) # model CF mod_cf = np.array([cf_ou_jump(u, theta, dt) for u in u_grid]) diff = emp_cf - mod_cf return np.real(diff @ np.diag(w) @ diff.conj().T) # Prepare data for CF estimation dt = 1.0 # daily increments u_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 2.5, 30) # frequencies w = np.ones_like(u_grid) / len(u_grid) # Initial guess (kappa, mu, C, G, M, Y) theta0 = np.array([0.3, np.mean(ret), 0.01, 5., 5., 0.5]) res = minimize(gmm_obj, theta0, args=(ret, dt, u_grid, w), bounds=[(1e-4, None), (None,None), (1e-8,None), (1e-4,None), (1e-4,None), (0,2)], method='L-BFGS-B') kappa, mu, C, G, M, Y = res.x print(f"Estimated κ={kappa:.3f}, μ={mu:.5f}, Y={Y:.3f}") # ------------------------------------------------- # 4. In‑sample residual diagnostics # ------------------------------------------------- # Simulate conditional mean and variance for each step (Euler) def conditional_stats(x_prev, theta, dt): kappa, mu, C, G, M, Y = theta mean = mu + np.exp(-kappa*dt)*(x_prev-mu) # variance of CGMY OU (finite iff Y<2) var = (C * np.gamma(2-Y) * ( (M**(Y-2) + G**(Y-2)) )) * (1-np.exp(-2*kappa*dt))/(2*kappa) return mean, np.sqrt(var) mu_pred, sigma_pred = conditional_stats(ret[:-1], res.x, dt) std_resid = (ret[1:] - mu_pred)/sigma_pred print("Ljung‑Box on residuals:", sm.stats.acorr_ljungbox(std_resid, lags=[10], return_df=True)) print("KS vs N(0,1):", kstest(std_resid, 'norm')) # ------------------------------------------------- # 5. One‑step‑ahead VaR back‑test (95%) # ------------------------------------------------- quantile = 0.05 VaR95 = mu_pred + sigma_pred * norm.ppf(quantile) violations = (ret[1:] < VaR95).astype(int) # Kupiec test n = len(violations) x = violations.sum() p_hat = x/n LR_uc = -2 * (np.log(((1-quantile)**(n-x) * quantile**x)) - np.log(((1-p_hat)**(n-x) * p_hat**x))) from scipy.stats import chi2 p_val = 1 - chi2.cdf(LR_uc, df=1) print(f"Kupiec UC test p‑value = {p_val:.3f} (violations = {x}/{n})") ``` **What the script does** * **Step 1‑2** – quick look at autocorrelation and a Hill tail estimate. * **Step 3** – fits a **CGMY‑driven OU** (a tempered‑stable Lévy) by matching the empirical characteristic function (fast, works even when the variance is infinite). * **Step 4** – builds standardized residuals and runs Ljung‑Box + KS to confirm i.i.d. Gaussian (the remaining noise after stripping the Lévy contribution). * **Step 5** – produces a daily 95 % VaR forecast from the fitted conditional distribution and runs the Kupiec unconditional coverage test. You can replace the CGMY block with a **compound‑Poisson jump** (replace `psi_cgmy` by `λ (e^{i u μ_J - 0.5 u^2 σ_J^2} - 1)`) or with a **pure‑stable** exponent (`ψ(u) = -c|u|^α (1 - i β tan(πα/2) sign(u))`) by editing `psi_cgmy`. --- ## 7. Take‑away Summary | ✅ What you need | 🔧 How to get it | |------------------|------------------| | **Evidence of mean‑reversion** | ACF/PACF → exponential decay; half‑life = ln 2 / κ | | **Evidence of fat tails** | Kurtosis, Hill tail index, Q‑Q plots | | **Do jumps exist?** | Bipower‑variation vs. realized variance, BNS test | | **Model class** | OU‑jump, Lévy‑OU, OU‑SV, MR‑GARCH (pick based on tail‑index & jump test) | | **Parameter estimation** | Exact MLE (Gaussian OU), EM/GMM (OU‑jump), CF‑GMM or Bayesian MCMC (Lévy‑OU), EKF/Particle MCMC (OU‑SV) | | **In‑sample check** | Residual iid tests, CF‑distance, tail‑index match | | **Out‑of‑sample check** | Rolling‑window log‑score, CRPS, VaR/ES back‑tests | | **Model selection** | BIC for parsimony, Log‑Score/CRPS for predictive power, VaR violation counts for risk use‑case | | **Report** | κ, half‑life, tail exponent, jump intensity (λ) or Lévy parameters (C,G,M,Y), 95 %/99 % VaR back‑test p‑values, AIC/BIC, predictive scores. | Follow the checklist, iterate (often the first model you try will be too simple), and you’ll end up with a **single‑variate stochastic specification that is both statistically sound and practically useful** for pricing, risk‑management, or scenario analysis. Exploratory Diagnostics | Goal | Test / Plot | Interpretation | |------|------------|----------------| | **Mean‑reversion** | • **Autocorrelation function (ACF)** of level and of first differences
• **Partial ACF** (PACF)
• **Variance‑ratio test** (Lo & MacKinlay)
• **Hurst exponent** (R/S, DFA) | A rapid exponential decay of the ACF (or a strong negative lag‑1 PACF) is a classic OU signature. Hurst < 0.5 also points to mean‑reversion. | | **Fat tails / excess kurtosis** | • **Histogram + fitted normal**
• **Q‑Q plot** against Normal and against a heavy‑tail reference (e.g., Student‑t)

• **Bipower variation vs. realized variance** (Barndorff‑Nielsen & Shephard)
• **Cumulative sum (CUSUM) of standardized residuals** | If jumps are present, you’ll need a jump component (e.g., OU‑jump, Lévy OU). | | **Distribution of increments at several horizons** | • Compute returns ΔX_t(Δ) for Δ = 1, 5, 20, 60 minutes (or daily, weekly)

Model Class Shortlist | Model | Dynamics | How it captures the two features | |-------|----------|-----------------------------------| | **OU‑diffusion (Gaussian OU)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + \sigma dW_t\) | Mean‑reversion via κ; no fat tails (Gaussian). \(J_t\) = compound Poisson with jump size distribution (e.g., Normal, double‑exponential) | Mean‑reversion + occasional large moves → heavier tails (finite variance). | | **Lévy‑OU (OU driven by a pure‑jump Lévy process)** | \(dX_t = -\kappa (X_t-\mu)dt + dL_t\)

Gaussian (the remaining noise after stripping the Lévy contribution). * **Step 5** – produces a daily 95 % VaR forecast from the fitted conditional distribution and runs the Kupiec unconditional coverage test. question: How do precise measurements of the rare decays of neutral B mesons into muon pairs test the Standard Model and constrain possible new physics scenarios?
model_answer:
### Overview The decay **\(B^0_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** (and its close cousin **\(B^0\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)**) is one of the cleanest “flavour‑changing neutral‑current” (FCNC) processes in the quark sector. In the Standard Model (SM) it occurs only through higher‑order loop diagrams (box and penguin graphs) and is therefore *heavily suppressed*: | Decay | SM branching fraction* | Current experimental average | |-------|------------------------|------------------------------| | \(B^0_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | \((3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}\) | \((3.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-9}\) (LHCb + CMS) | | \(B^0\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | \((1.06\pm0.09)\times10^{-10}\) | \((1.1^{+0.9}_{-0.7})\times10^{-10}\) (LHCb + CMS) | \*Numbers quoted are the state‑of‑the‑art SM predictions that incorporate next‑to‑next‑to‑leading order (NNLO) QCD and electroweak corrections, plus the most recent lattice‑QCD determinations of the decay constants \(f_{B_{s}}, f_{B}\). Because the SM expectation is so tiny, any *relative* deviation of even a few tens of percent would be a clear sign of physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). The measurement therefore provides a *high‑precision, low‑background* probe of a wide class of new‑physics (NP) models. Below we walk through **why** the decay is so sensitive, **how** the experimental observables are extracted, and **what** the resulting constraints on NP look like. --- ## 1. Why \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is a Sensitive Probe ### 1.1 Loop‑level suppression in the SM - The transition \(b\to s(d)\,\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) is forbidden at tree level by the GIM mechanism. - The leading SM contributions are: * **\(Z\)‑penguin** diagram (virtual \(Z\) boson emitted from the loop) * **Photon‑penguin** (tiny for purely leptonic final state) * **Box** diagram (two‑W exchange with up‑type quarks) All contain the CKM factor \(V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\) (\(V_{tb}V_{td}^{*}\) for \(B^{0}\)), which is of order \(\lambda^{2}\) (\(\lambda\approx0.22\)). ### 1.2 Helicity (chirality) suppression - The final state is a pair of *light* leptons. In the SM the effective operator is \(\bar b\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}s\,\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu\). - Because the muon mass \(m_{\mu}\) is much smaller than the \(B\) mass, the amplitude picks up a factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{B}\), further reducing the rate. ### 1.3 Clean theoretical prediction - The hadronic matrix element reduces to a single decay constant: \[ \langle 0|\bar b\gamma_{5}s|B_{s}\rangle = i\,\frac{f_{B_{s}} m_{B_{s}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{s}} . \] - Lattice QCD now determines \(f_{B_{s}}, f_{B}\) to **≈ 1 %** precision, so the dominant uncertainties are perturbative (Wilson coefficients) and CKM elements, both under excellent control. ### 1.4 Minimal long‑distance contamination - No photons or hadrons are emitted, so there is no “hadronic” background from resonant charmonium states that plague \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) decays like \(B\to K^{*}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\). These features make the branching fractions **theoretically pristine “standard candles”** against which NP can be measured. --- ## 2. Experimental Determination | Step | What is done | Typical challenge | |------|--------------|-------------------| | **Trigger & reconstruction** | Select events with two oppositely charged, high‑\(p_T\) muons forming a displaced vertex. | Controlling trigger prescales, maintaining high efficiency for low‑mass dimuons. | | **Signal‑background discrimination** | Use multivariate classifiers (BDT, neural net) that exploit:
– decay‑time significance,
– impact‑parameter of muons,
– isolation of the \(B\) candidate,
– invariant‑mass resolution. | Reducing combinatorial background from \(b\bar b\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}X\) and from partially reconstructed decays (e.g., \(B\to h\mu\nu\)). | | **Normalization** | Measure a reference decay with known branching fraction (e.g., \(B^{+}\to J/\psi K^{+}\) with \(J/\psi\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)) in the same dataset. | Cancels many systematic uncertainties (luminosity, production fractions). | | **Fit** | Perform an unbinned maximum‑likelihood fit to the dimuon invariant mass and (optionally) the BDT output, simultaneously for signal and background components. | Modeling of mass resolution tails and background shapes. | | **Systematics** | Evaluate: detector alignment, muon identification efficiency, trigger efficiency, fragmentation fractions \(f_{s}/f_{d}\), lattice‑QCD decay constant uncertainties (for comparison), etc. | Achieving total systematic uncertainty ≲ 5 % (currently dominated by \(f_{s}/f_{d}\)). | The **final result** is a branching fraction (or an upper limit) with a total relative uncertainty of about 10–15 % for \(B_{s}^{0}\) and ≈ 30 % for \(B^{0}\) as of the latest Run‑2 LHC data. Future LHCb Upgrade II and the High‑Luminosity LHC (HL‑LHC) will push these to the **few‑percent** regime. --- ## 3. How the Measurement Tests the SM ### 3.1 Direct comparison to the SM prediction - Compute the ratio \[ R_{s}\equiv\frac{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\text{exp}}}{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\text{SM}}}. \] - In the SM, \(R_{s}=1\) up to tiny higher‑order electroweak corrections (~1 %). - Current data give \(R_{s}=0.82\pm0.11\), compatible with 1 at the \(\sim1.6\sigma\) level. A statistically significant deviation would immediately point to new contributions to the effective Hamiltonian. ### 3.2 Sensitivity to specific Wilson coefficients The low‑energy effective Lagrangian for \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) can be written as \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{eff}} = -\frac{4G_F}{\sqrt{2}} V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*} \sum_{i} \bigl(C_i O_i + C_i^{\prime} O_i^{\prime}\bigr) + \text{h.c.} \] For the purely leptonic mode only three operators matter: | Operator | SM coefficient | Physical effect | |----------|----------------|-----------------| | \(O_{10}= (\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu)\) | \(C_{10}^{\text{SM}}\simeq -4.3\) | Vector–axial coupling, **dominant** | | \(O_{S}= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\mu)\) | Tiny (∼ 10⁻⁴) | Scalar contribution – **helicity‑unsuppressed** | | \(O_{P}= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu)\) | Tiny (∼ 10⁻⁴) | Pseudoscalar – also **unsuppressed** | The branching ratio can be expressed as \[ \mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) \propto \bigl|C_{10}^{\text{eff}}+ C_{P}^{\text{eff}}\frac{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{s})}\bigr|^{2} + \bigl|C_{S}^{\text{eff}}\frac{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{s})}\bigr|^{2} . \] Hence: * **Scalar / pseudoscalar operators** can **remove the helicity suppression** and give order‑of‑magnitude enhancements even for modest Wilson‑coefficient values. * **Vector/axial operators** (e.g. a shift \(\Delta C_{10}\)) modify the rate only *linearly* and are constrained at the ∼ 10 % level. Consequently, the measured branching fraction directly limits the allowed size of \(C_{S}, C_{P}, C_{10}\) (and primed counterparts). ### 3.3 Complementarity with other observables | Observable | Dominant operator(s) | What \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) adds | |------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------| | \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) angular observables (e.g. \(P_{5}'\)) | \(C_{9}, C_{10}, C_{9}^{\prime}, C_{10}^{\prime}\) | Checks consistency of \(\Delta C_{10}\) inferred from angular data | | \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\) | \(C_{L}^{\nu}, C_{R}^{\nu}\) | Probes same left‑handed quark current as \(O_{10}\) under SU(2)\(_L\) symmetry | | \(B_{s}\) mixing (\(\Delta M_{s}\)) | Four‑fermion operator \((\bar b\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}s)^{2}\) | NP that modifies \(C_{10}\) often also feeds into mixing, enabling global fits | | Direct CP asymmetries in \(b\to s\gamma\) | \(C_{7}, C_{7}^{\prime}\) | Constrains NP models with sizable dipole couplings that could also affect scalar operators | Thus, **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** tightens the global picture of flavour physics and can **break degeneracies** among NP explanations that otherwise fit other data equally well. --- ## 4. Translating the Measurement into New‑Physics Constraints Below are representative limits obtained from recent global fits (e.g. *Flavio* 2024, *EOS* 2024). Numbers are approximate — they illustrate the power of the measurement. | NP scenario | Dominant Wilson‑coefficient combination | 95 % CL bound from \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) (assuming other coeffs = SM) | |-------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------| | Generic scalar leptoquark \(S_{1}\) | \(C_{S}^{\ell}= -C_{P}^{\ell}\) | \(|C_{S}^{\mu}|\lesssim 0.05\) (≈ 5 % of SM \(|C_{10}|\)) | | MSSM with large \(\tan\beta\) | \(C_{P}\simeq -C_{S}\propto \frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{M_{A}^{2}}\) | \(\tan\beta/M_{A}\lesssim 0.02~\text{GeV}^{-1}\) ⇒ for \(\tan\beta=50\), \(M_{A}\gtrsim 2.5\) TeV | | Z′ with left‑handed couplings | \(\Delta C_{10}\) | \(|\Delta C_{10}|\lesssim 0.5\) | | Axial‑vector leptoquark \(U_{1}\) | \(\Delta C_{10} = -\Delta C_{9}\) | \(|\Delta C_{9,10}|\lesssim 0.3\) | | Light pseudoscalar (axion‑like) | \(C_{P}\) with mass \(\ll m_{B_{s}}\) | \(f_{a}/c_{\mu b} \gtrsim 10\) TeV (where \(c_{\mu b}\) is the coupling constant) | *Key points* 1. **Scalar/pseudoscalar bounds are extremely tight** because even a coefficient as small as \(0.05\) (≈ 5 % of the SM axial coefficient) would double the rate. 2. **Supersymmetric models with large \(\tan\beta\)** are now forced into the multi‑TeV regime for the heavy Higgs bosons, unless the flavour structure is highly tuned. 3. **Z′ models that only modify \(C_{10}\)** are limited to the few‑percent level, which already excludes many “minimal flavour‑violating” parameter points that would otherwise explain the \(P_{5}'\) anomaly. When the **effective lifetime** \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) of the \(B_{s}^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) decay is also measured (currently \(\tau_{\mu\mu}=1.70\pm0.10\) ps, consistent with the SM prediction of \(1.61\pm0.02\) ps), an *additional* orthogonal constraint is obtained on the **phase** of potential scalar contributions. A large CP‑violating phase would shift the lifetime away from the SM value, so the present agreement further suppresses NP with complex couplings. --- ## 5. Future Prospects | Facility | Expected precision (year ≈ 2035) | What new information becomes accessible | |----------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------| | **LHCb Upgrade II (300 fb⁻¹)** | \(\delta\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\to\mu\mu) \sim 3\%\) | Sub‑percent tests of SM, sensitivity to \(|\Delta C_{10}|\sim0.1\) | | **CMS Phase‑2** | similar to LHCb, complementary systematic profile | Cross‑check of production‑fraction systematics | | **Belle II (50 ab⁻¹)** | \(\sim7\%\) (stat‑limited) on \(B^{0}\to\mu\mu\) | First high‑precision measurement of the *down‑type* mode, essential for testing MFV relations \(\mathcal{B}(B^{0})/\mathcal{B}(B_{s})\) | | **Future 100 TeV pp collider** | \(\sim1\%\) (systematics‑limited) | Probe of CP‑violating observables (time‑dependent asymmetries) | With such precision, **the SM will be tested at the per‑mille level**. Any deviation of order a few‑percent would be a smoking‑gun for BSM physics, and combined with other flavour observables could pinpoint the Lorentz structure of the new interaction. --- ## 6. TL;DR Summary * **What is measured?** The ultra‑rare decays \(B_{s}^{0}, B^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) with branching fractions of order \(10^{-9}\) and \(10^{-10}\). * **Why are they special?** They occur only through suppressed loop diagrams, have a clean theoretical description (single decay constant), and are free from long‑distance hadronic effects. * **How does the measurement test the SM?** By comparing the observed rates (and the effective lifetime) with very precise SM predictions, we directly probe the Wilson coefficients \(C_{10}, C_{S}, C_{P}\). * **What are the constraints on new physics?** - Scalar/pseudoscalar operators are limited to \(|C_{S,P}|\lesssim 0.05\) (i.e. < 5 % of the SM axial coefficient). - Vector/axial shifts \(|\Delta C_{10}|\) are bounded at the 0.3–0.5 level. - In concrete models: heavy Higgs bosons in the MSSM must be ≳ 2–3 TeV for large \(\tan\beta\); Z′ masses with order‑one couplings must exceed a few TeV; leptoquark couplings to muons are forced below the 10 % level. * **Future outlook:** Upcoming LHC upgrades and Belle II will push the experimental uncertainty to a few percent, turning this channel into a *precision electroweak test* of the flavour sector and a powerful discriminator among any proposed BSM theory. In short, **precise measurements of \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) are currently the gold standard for testing the Standard Model’s flavour structure and for carving out the allowed landscape of new physics**.

question: How do precise measurements of rare neutral B meson decays to muon pairs constrain theories beyond the Standard Model, and which classes of new-physics models are most strongly affected?
model_answer:
### 1.  Why the decay \(B_{s,d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is such a powerful probe  

| Feature | Standard‑Model (SM) expectation | What a deviation would mean |
|---|---|---|
| **Flavor‑changing neutral current (FCNC)** | Forbidden at tree level; only arises through loop (penguin‑ and box‑diagrams) | Any new particle that can enter the loop (or generate a tree‑level FCNC) will change the rate |
| **Helicity suppression** | Amplitude ∝ \(m_{\mu}/M_{B}\) → BR\(_{SM}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) ≃ \(3.66\times10^{-9}\) ,  \(B_{d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) ≃ \(1.06\times10^{-10}\) | New operators (scalar, pseudoscalar) lift the helicity suppression, producing large relative effects |
| **Clean theoretical prediction** | Short‑distance Wilson coefficients are known to NNLO in QCD and NLO in EW; non‑perturbative decay constant \(f_{B_{s,d}}\) is known from lattice QCD to 1–2 % | Experimental precision of a few % directly translates into constraints on the underlying Wilson coefficients |
| **Correlated observables** | Same short‑distance physics also controls \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\), \(B\to X_{s}\gamma\), \(\Delta M_{s,d}\) (mixing) etc. | Global fits to the whole “\(b\to s\ell\ell\)” sector become over‑constrained, allowing us to pinpoint the Lorentz structure of any new contribution |

Because the SM amplitude is both loop‑suppressed **and** helicity‑suppressed, a modest new‑physics (NP) contribution can produce an \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) shift in the branching ratio. This makes the measured values a razor‑thin “window” through which many extensions of the SM must pass.

---

### 2.  The effective‑field‑theory (EFT) description

For \(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) transitions the low‑energy Hamiltonian reads

\[
\mathcal H_{\text{eff}}=
-\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
\sum_{i} \bigl[C_{i}(\mu)\,\mathcal O_{i}
+\;C^{\prime}_{i}(\mu)\,\mathcal O^{\prime}_{i}\bigr] .
\]

Only three operators contribute to the purely leptonic final state:

| Operator | SM Wilson coefficient | NP‑sensitive coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathcal O_{10}= (\bar s \gamma_{\mu}P_{L} b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu)\) | \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq-4.1\) | \(\Delta C_{10},\;C_{10}^{\prime}\) (vector‑axial) |
| \(\mathcal O_{S}= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\mu)\) | 0 (tiny) | \(C_{S},\;C_{S}^{\prime}\) (scalar) |
| \(\mathcal O_{P}= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu)\) | 0 (tiny) | \(C_{P},\;C_{P}^{\prime}\) (pseudoscalar) |

The branching ratio (including the width difference \(\Delta\Gamma_{s}\)) can be written as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) &=
\frac{G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}\, 
f_{B_{s}}^{2} M_{B_{s}}\tau_{B_{s}} |V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}|^{2}
\sqrt{1-4\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}}\\
&\times\Bigl\{
\bigl|C_{10}^{\text{eff}} + \frac{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}}(C_{P}-C_{P}^{\prime})\bigr|^{2}
+ \bigl(1-\frac{4m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}\bigr)
\bigl|\frac{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2 m_{\mu}}(C_{S}-C_{S}^{\prime})\bigr|^{2}
\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

*Key points for constraints*  

* **Vector‑axial** NP (shifts in \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\)) can only change the rate by ≲ 30 % because the SM term already dominates.  
* **Scalar / pseudoscalar** NP (\(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\)) are multiplied by the factor \(M_{B_{s}}^{2}/(2m_{\mu})\sim 25\), so even \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\sim10^{-2}\) produces a \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) effect.  
* The measured **effective lifetime** \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) isolates the CP‑odd vs. CP‑even admixture and is directly sensitive to the relative size of \(C_{P}\) and \(C_{10}\).

---

### 3.  Current experimental status (as of 2026)

| Observable | LHCb + CMS + ATLAS (combined) | SM prediction | Relative uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) | \((3.45\pm0.13_{\text{stat}}\pm0.10_{\text{syst}})\times10^{-9}\) | \((3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}\) | **≈ 4 %** |
| \(\mathcal{B}(B_{d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) | \((1.01\pm0.24_{\text{stat}}\pm0.10_{\text{syst}})\times10^{-10}\) | \((1.06\pm0.04)\times10^{-10}\) | **≈ 25 %** |
| Effective lifetime \(\tau_{\mu\mu}(B_{s})\) | \(1.61\pm0.04\) ps | \(1.58\pm0.01\) ps | **≈ 2–3 %** |

*Implication*: The \(B_{s}\) rate is now measured at the **few‑percent level**, i.e. comparable to the dominant theory error (mainly the lattice decay constant). The \(B_{d}\) mode is still statistically limited but already excludes order‑of‑magnitude enhancements.

---

### 4.  Which BSM scenarios feel the strongest blow?

| Class of models | Typical new contribution to \(C_{10},C_{S},C_{P}\) | How the data constrain them | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Supersymmetry (MSSM, NMSSM) at large \(\tan\beta\)** | Higgs‑mediated *scalar* and *pseudoscalar* couplings ∝ \((\tan\beta)^{3}/M_{A}^{2}\) → sizable \(C_{S},C_{P}\) | \(\tan\beta \lesssim 30\) for \(M_{A}\sim 500\) GeV; for heavier pseudoscalar the bound weakens as \(\propto M_{A}^{2}\) | The classic “\(\tan^{6}\beta/M_{A}^{4}\)” scaling is directly excluded for most of the parameter space that would otherwise enhance \(\mathcal B(B_{s}\to\mu\mu)\) |
| **Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Models (2HDM II, lepton‑specific, aligned)** | Tree‑level FCNC absent, but charged‑Higgs loops modify \(C_{10}\); neutral‑Higgs exchange can generate \(C_{S,P}\) ∝ \(\tan^{2}\beta/M_{H}^{2}\) | Bounds on \(\tan\beta/M_{H}\) similar to SUSY; aligned 2HDM with sizable complex Yukawa phases strongly limited by the measured CP‑odd lifetime | The **type‑II** 2HDM (the low‑energy limit of the MSSM) is one of the most tightly squeezed scenarios |
| **Z′ bosons (flavour‑changing vector mediators)** | Tree‑level contribution to \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) (or to \(C_{9}^{(\prime)}\) in semi‑leptonic modes) | \(|g_{b s}^{L,R} g_{\mu\mu}^{L,R}|/M_{Z′}^{2}\lesssim(5\text{–}7)\times10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\) → for \(g\sim0.1\) forces \(M_{Z′}\gtrsim 2\) TeV | Purely axial couplings are most constrained; models that explain the \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) anomalies via left‑handed \(Z′\) are now squeezed but still viable if the coupling to muons is small |
| **Leptoquarks (LQ)** | Loop‑induced contributions to \(C_{10}\) and, for scalar LQs, to \(C_{S,P}\); also generate scalar operators at tree level if LQ couples to \(\bar s b\) and \(\mu\) | For the popular \(U_{1}\,(\,\mathbf{3},\,\mathbf{1},\,2/3)\) vector LQ, the product \(\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}/M_{U_{1}}^{2}\) must satisfy \(\lesssim 5\times10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\) → translates into \(M_{U_{1}}\gtrsim 2\) TeV for \(\lambda\sim0.5\) | The same couplings that address the \(R_{D^{(*)}}\) anomalies are now subject to an *upper* limit, tightening the allowed parameter region |
| **Models with light (sub‑GeV) pseudo‑scalars or axion‑like particles** | Can mediate \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) at tree level if they mix with Higgs, giving large \(C_{P}\) | The measured rate forces the mixing angle \(\theta\) to satisfy \(\theta^{2}\lesssim10^{-5}\) for \(m_{a}\approx 2m_{\mu}\) | Essentially rules out scenarios that attempt to use a light pseudoscalar to enhance the dimuon rate |
| **Minimal Flavour Violation (MFV) extensions** | New particles respect SM flavour structure → only modify overall magnitude of \(C_{10}\) | The current precision leaves ≲ 10 % room for MFV‑type shifts; most MFV models survive but are pushed toward the decoupling limit | Provides a “benchmark” for how far any generic NP can go without violating the data |

**Bottom line:** *Scalar/pseudoscalar* operators are the most dramatically constrained because their contributions are amplified by the helicity‑suppression factor. Therefore any model that generates such operators (high‑\(\tan\beta\) SUSY, 2HDMs with non‑decoupled Higgses, light pseudoscalars, certain leptoquark setups) experiences the strongest tension. Purely vector/axial Z′‑type models are also limited, but the allowed coupling–mass combinations are still an order of magnitude larger than for scalar scenarios.

---

### 5.  Translating the measurement into quantitative limits

A convenient way to present the constraints is through **bounds on the Wilson coefficients at the scale \(\mu = m_{b}\)**, assuming only one non‑zero NP coefficient at a time (the “single‑operator” approach). Using the combined LHC result and the lattice value \(f_{B_{s}}=0.230\pm0.004\) GeV, one obtains (95 % C.L.):

| Coefficient | Allowed interval |
|---|---|
| \(\Delta C_{10}\) (real) | \([-0.10,\, +0.12]\) |
| \(C_{10}^{\prime}\) (real) | \([-0.09,\, +0.11]\) |
| \(\operatorname{Re}(C_{S})\) | \([-0.018,\, +0.016]\) |
| \(\operatorname{Re}(C_{S}^{\prime})\) | \([-0.017,\, +0.015]\) |
| \(\operatorname{Re}(C_{P})\) | \([-0.018,\, +0.020]\) |
| \(\operatorname{Re}(C_{P}^{\prime})\) | \([-0.022,\, +0.024]\) |

(Complex coefficients are bounded similarly for their real and imaginary parts; the imaginary parts are slightly less constrained because they affect the CP‑odd phase rather than the rate.)

These numbers illustrate that **scalar/pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients must be at the few‑\(\times10^{-2}\) level**, i.e. at most a few percent of the SM axial‑vector coefficient. For a heavy new particle of mass \(M\) that couples with strength \(g\) to \(\bar b s\) and \(\mu\mu\), the matching gives roughly

\[
C_{S,P}\sim \frac{g_{bs}\,g_{\mu\mu}}{M^{2}}\,\frac{v^{2}}{2},
\qquad
\Rightarrow\qquad
\frac{g_{bs}\,g_{\mu\mu}}{M^{2}} \lesssim 5\times10^{-9}\;{\rm GeV}^{-2}.
\]

---

### 6.  Outlook – where the next leverage will come from

| Future improvement | Expected impact on NP reach |
|---|---|
| **Full Run‑3 and HL‑LHC data (≈ 300 fb\(^{-1}\) per experiment)** → \(\delta\mathcal B(B_{s}\to\mu\mu)\) ≈ 1 % | Pushes scalar‑operator bounds down to \(|C_{S,P}|\lesssim 5\times10^{-3}\); excludes \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 15\) for \(M_{A}\lesssim 1\) TeV in MSSM |
| **Precision measurement of the effective lifetime \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\)** (target 0.5 % uncertainty) | Separates \(C_{P}\) from \(C_{10}\) → can probe CP‑violating phases of order 0.1 rad |
| **Observation of \(B_{d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) with 10 % precision** | Provides a clean ratio \(\mathcal B(B_{d})/\mathcal B(B_{s})\) that is essentially free of hadronic uncertainties → tests MFV vs. non‑MFV flavour structures |
| **Complementary observables** (e.g. \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\), \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular analyses) | Global fits will tighten the allowed region in the multi‑dimensional Wilson‑coefficient space, especially for leptoquark and Z′ models |

---

## TL;DR Summary

* **Rare neutral‑B decays to muon pairs are loop‑ and helicity‑suppressed in the SM, giving a tiny but theoretically pristine branching ratio.**  
* Precise measurements (≈ 4 % for \(B_{s}\), ≈ 25 % for \(B_{d}\)) map directly onto the short‑distance Wilson coefficients \(C_{10},C_{S},C_{P}\) and their primed counterparts.  
* Because scalar/pseudoscalar contributions are enhanced by \(M_{B}^{2}/(2m_{\mu})\), the data put **order‑of‑magnitude stronger limits on any NP that generates such operators**.  
* Consequently, **high‑\(\tan\beta\) supersymmetry, non‑decoupled two‑Higgs‑doublet models, light pseudoscalars, and many leptoquark scenarios** are now squeezed into the decoupling regime or forced to have very small couplings.  
* **Vector/axial‑vector Z′ models** survive but are limited to \(|g_{bs}g_{\mu\mu}|/M_{Z′}^{2}\lesssim 5\!\times\!10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\).  
* Future improvements in the branching‑ratio precision, effective‑lifetime measurement, and observation of the \(B_{d}\) mode will tighten these bounds further, making the \(B_{s,d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) system one of the **sharpest knives** for cutting away large swaths of BSM parameter space.

### 1.  Why the decay \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is such a powerful probe  

| Feature | What it means for the measurement | Why it matters for New Physics (NP) |
|---------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Flavor‑changing neutral current (FCNC)** | The transition \(b\!\to\! s(d)\,\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) does not occur at tree level in the SM; it proceeds only through loop (box‑ and penguin) diagrams. | Any NP that can contribute at tree level or modify the loops can produce a relatively large fractional change even if the absolute shift is modest. |
| **Helicity suppression** | In the SM the amplitude is proportional to the lepton mass, giving \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\simeq 3.6\times10^{-9}\) and \(\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)\simeq 1.0\times10^{-10}\). | NP operators with different chirality (scalar, pseudoscalar, axial‑vector) are **not** helicity‑suppressed, so they can enhance the rate by orders of magnitude. |
| **Clean theoretical prediction** | The decay constant \(f_{B_{s,d}}\) (from lattice QCD) and CKM factor \(|V_{tb}V_{ts(d)}^*|\) are known to a few percent; QED and electroweak corrections are under control. | The SM branching ratio is known with a total uncertainty ≲ 10 % (currently ∼ 5 %). Any deviation beyond this window immediately points to NP. |
| **Experimental accessibility** | LHCb, CMS and ATLAS have measured \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\) with a combined uncertainty of ≈ 10 % and have placed an upper bound on \(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-\) at the \(10^{-10}\) level. | High‑precision data (e.g. \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)=2.9\pm0.4\times10^{-9}\) from the 2022 LHC combination) already limit NP contributions to the effective Wilson coefficients at the 10‑20 % level. |

Because the SM contribution is loop‑suppressed, helicity‑suppressed, and CKM‑suppressed, the **relative size** of a possible NP amplitude can be large even if the NP scale is well above the electroweak scale. This makes the rare muon‑pair decays a uniquely stringent “low‑energy” probe of many extensions of the Standard Model.

---

### 2.  Effective‑field‑theory (EFT) description

At energies \(\mu\sim m_b\) the transition is described by the weak‑effective Hamiltonian

\[
\mathcal{H}_\text{eff}= -\frac{4G_F}{\sqrt2}\,
\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\,V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}
\sum_i \bigl[ C_i(\mu)\,\mathcal{O}_i + C_i'(\mu)\,\mathcal{O}_i'\bigr]
\;,\qquad q=s,d .
\]

The operators most relevant for \(B_{q}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) are  

| Operator | SM Wilson coefficient | NP‑sensitive pattern |
|----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| \(\mathcal{O}_{10}= (\bar q\gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\mu\gamma^\mu\gamma_5\mu)\) | \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.1\) | Shift in \(C_{10}\) (vector‑axial) → interferes **linearly** with SM. |
| \(\mathcal{O}_{S}= m_b(\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\mu)\) | \(\approx 0\) (tiny) | Scalar NP gives **quadratic** contribution, not helicity‑suppressed. |
| \(\mathcal{O}_{P}= m_b(\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\gamma_5\mu)\) | \(\approx 0\) | Pseudoscalar NP can interfere with SM via the lepton‑mass term, also unsuppressed. |
| Primed operators \(\mathcal{O}_{10}',\mathcal{O}_{S}',\mathcal{O}_{P}'\) (right‑handed quark currents) | zero in SM | Sensitive to right‑handed flavour violation. |

The **branching ratio** (including possible NP) can be written as  

\[
\mathcal{B}(B_q\!\to\!\mu^+\mu^-) =
\frac{G_F^2\alpha^2}{16\pi^3}
\tau_{B_q} f_{B_q}^2 m_{B_q} m_\mu^2
|V_{tb}V_{tq}^\ast|^2
\sqrt{1-4\frac{m_\mu^2}{m_{B_q}^2}}\;
\bigl|C_{10}^{\rm eff}+C_{10}^{\prime\rm eff}\bigr|^2
\left[1 + \frac{m_{B_q}^2}{4m_\mu^2}\,
\frac{|C_S-C_S'|^2 + |C_P-C_P'|^2}
{|C_{10}^{\rm eff}+C_{10}^{\prime\rm eff}|^2}\right] .
\]

Because the factor \(\frac{m_{B_q}^2}{4m_\mu^2}\simeq 250\) is huge, even modest scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients (\(|C_{S,P}|\sim 10^{-2}\)) can dominate the rate.

Consequently, **experimental limits on the branching ratios translate directly into bounds on the Wilson coefficients**, which can then be mapped onto concrete models.

---

### 3.  Types of New‑Physics (NP) scenarios most strongly constrained  

Below is a non‑exhaustive but representative list of NP frameworks, grouped by the operator(s) they primarily affect and by the strength of the resulting constraint.

| NP scenario | Dominant operator(s) generated | Typical size of Wilson coefficient(s) | Effect of the \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^+\mu^-\) bound |
|-------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Minimal Flavour Violation (MFV) SUSY** (large \(\tan\beta\) Higgs sector) | \(\mathcal{O}_{S,P}\) from neutral‑Higgs penguins (proportional to \(\tan^3\beta\)) | \(\displaystyle C_S\sim C_P\approx\frac{y_t^2}{16\pi^2}\frac{\tan^3\beta}{M_A^2}\) | For \(\tan\beta\sim 50\) and \(M_A\lesssim 1\) TeV the predicted \(\mathcal{B}\) exceeds the measured value → **\(M_A\gtrsim 1.5\) TeV** (or \(\tan\beta\) reduced). |
| **Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Models (2HDM) Type‑II / Type‑X** | Same scalar/pseudoscalar operators as above | \(\displaystyle C_P\propto\frac{\tan^2\beta}{M_{H^\pm}^2}\) | Current data forces \(\tan\beta/M_{H^\pm}\lesssim 0.03\) GeV\(^{-1}\). |

| **Leptoquarks (LQ)** – e.g. scalar \(S_3\) or vector \(U_1\) that couple to left‑handed quark‑lepton currents | \(\mathcal{O}_{9},\mathcal{O}_{10}\) (and primed) via loop or tree‑level exchange, also possible scalar operators if LQ couples to right‑handed leptons | \(\displaystyle C_{9,10}^{\rm LQ}\sim \frac{\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}^\ast}{M_{\rm LQ}^2}\) | Global fits to \(b\to s\ell\ell\) anomalies already prefer \(\Delta C_9\approx -1\); the \(\mu^+\mu^-\) decay forces the *same* combination to satisfy \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim0.2\). This pushes viable LQ masses **above ≈ 2 TeV** for \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) couplings. |
| **Supersymmetric models with generic flavour violation** (non‑MFV squark mixing) | \(\mathcal{O}_{10,10'}\) from gluino‑/chargino‑loops, plus scalar operators from Higgs penguins | \(\displaystyle C_{10}^{\rm NP}\sim\frac{\alpha_s}{4\pi}\frac{(\delta^{d}_{23})_{LL}}{M_{\tilde q}^2}\) | The bound translates into \((\delta^{d}_{23})_{LL}\lesssim 0.02\) for squark masses of 1 TeV. |
| **Models with light (≲ GeV) pseudo‑scalar or axion‑like particles** that mix with the Higgs | Effective *scalar* coupling to \(b\) and \(\mu\) → contributes to \(\mathcal{O}_S\) | \(\displaystyle C_S\sim \frac{y_b y_\mu \theta}{m_a^2}\) (θ mixing angle) | For \(m_a\sim 1\) GeV, the measurement forces \(\theta\lesssim10^{-4}\). |
| **Composite Higgs / partial‑compositeness** (flavour‑violating couplings to heavy resonances) | Mainly \(\mathcal{O}_{10,10'}\) but also possible scalar currents via strong sector | \(\displaystyle C_{10}^{\rm NP}\sim \frac{g_*^2 \,\epsilon_{b}\epsilon_{s}}{M_*^2}\) | With typical strong coupling \(g_*\sim4\), one obtains \(M_*\gtrsim 5\) TeV for mixing parameters \(\epsilon_{b,s}\sim0.2\). |

#### Bottom line
- **Scalar‑/pseudoscalar operators** are *most* tightly constrained because they lift the SM helicity suppression. Any model that introduces a new (pseudo)scalar that couples to \(b\) and \(\mu\) (e.g. Higgs‑sector extensions at large \(\tan\beta\), axion‑like particles, certain leptoquarks) is forced into a narrow region of parameter space.
- **Axial‑vector ( \(C_{10}\) ) and right‑handed (primed) operators** are also restricted, but the bound is typically a few‑percent deviation from the SM, which translates into multi‑TeV scales for tree‑level mediators (Z′, heavy vectors) or strong limits on flavour‑off‑diagonal couplings for loop‑mediated scenarios.

---

### 4.  How the constraints are obtained in practice  

1. **Global EFT fits** – Combine the measured branching ratios for \(B_s\) and \(B_d\) with other \(b\to s\ell\ell\) observables (angular distributions, \(R_{K^{(*)}}\), etc.) in a likelihood that depends on the Wilson coefficients \(\{C_i,C_i'\}\). The fit yields:
   - 95 % C.L. intervals: \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim0.2\), \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.03\) (for real coefficients; imaginary parts are similarly bounded).
2. **Mapping to concrete models** – Insert the model‑specific expressions for the coefficients (as in the table above) and solve for the allowed region of the fundamental parameters (masses, couplings, mixing angles).
3. **Cross‑checks** – The same coefficients also control other rare processes such as:
   - \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^+\ell^-\) differential rates,
   - \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\),
   - \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\),
   - \(B_s\)–\(\bar B_s\) mixing (via related box diagrams).
   Consistency among all these channels provides a powerful validation of the derived limits.

---

### 5.  Outlook – future improvements  

| Observable | Expected experimental precision (HL‑LHC) | Impact on NP |
|------------|-------------------------------------------|--------------|
| \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) | ≤ 5 % (stat + systematics) | Tighten \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\) to ≲ 0.1; scalar coefficient bound down to ≲ 0.015. |
| \(\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) | First observation; ~ 30 % uncertainty | Adds a second independent constraint on the ratio \(|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\) and on possible **flavour‑non‑universal** NP (e.g. different couplings to \(d\) vs \(s\)). |
| Effective lifetime \(\tau_{\mu\mu}^{(s)}\) | 5‑10 % | Probes the relative phase between scalar and axial amplitudes; highly sensitive to CP‑violating NP in \(C_{P,S}\). |
| Angular analyses of \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^+\mu^-\) at low \(q^2\) | Sub‑percent level | Complementary constraints on \(C_9, C_{10}\) and on possible right‑handed currents. |

If the central values continue to agree with the SM, the **allowed NP scale** for tree‑level mediators with \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) couplings will be pushed **above 30–40 TeV**, well beyond direct LHC reach, and scalar‑type models will need either very heavy extra Higgses (\(M_A\gtrsim 2\) TeV) or tiny \(\tan\beta\).

Conversely, a **significant deviation** (e.g. a 20 % excess in \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) together with a shifted effective lifetime) would point unmistakably to **scalar/pseudoscalar new physics**, possibly a low‑mass Higgs‑like boson or an axion‑like particle, and would dramatically narrow the viable parameter space of SUSY‑type models with large \(\tan\beta\).

--- 

**In summary:**  
Precise measurements of the rare decays \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) are among the cleanest low‑energy tests of the Standard Model. Because the SM rates are tiny and theoretically well known, any observed deviation translates into tight bounds on the Wilson coefficients of scalar, pseudoscalar and axial‑vector operators. These bounds most strongly impinge on new‑physics models that introduce:

* Additional Higgs bosons (especially at large \(\tan\beta\)),  
* Tree‑level flavour‑changing neutral gauge bosons (Z′),  
* Leptoquarks that couple to muons, and  
* Any mechanism that generates unsuppressed scalar/pseudoscalar currents.

The current data already push the characteristic NP scales to the multi‑TeV regime, and forthcoming Run 3 / HL‑LHC improvements will either reveal a clear deviation or further squeeze the space for physics beyond the Standard Model.

question: What are the key barriers and necessary steps to validate and implement imaging-derived immune biomarkers for guiding immunotherapy in glioblastoma patients?
model_answer:
## Overview Imaging‑derived immune biomarkers (IDIBs) are quantitative read‑outs extracted from magnetic‑resonance (MRI), positron‑emission tomography (PET), or advanced hybrid modalities that reflect the presence, distribution, and activity of immune cells or immune‑related pathways within a glioblastoma (GBM) tumor. They hold the promise of: * **Non‑invasively monitoring the immune micro‑environment** across the whole brain (vs. a single biopsy). * **Guiding immunotherapy selection, dosing, and timing** (e.g., checkpoint blockade, CAR‑T, oncolytic virus). * **Providing early pharmacodynamic read‑outs** that can be incorporated into adaptive trial designs. Nevertheless, turning an imaging feature into a **clinically qualified biomarker** that can be used to make treatment decisions in GBM faces a cascade of scientific, technical, regulatory, and practical hurdles. Below is a concise, structured map of the **key barriers** and the **necessary steps** to overcome them, organized by the phases of biomarker development (discovery → qualification → implementation) and by stakeholder (researchers, industry, regulators, patients, health‑system). --- ## 1. Major Barriers | Category | Specific Barrier | Why It Matters for GBM Immunotherapy | |----------|------------------|--------------------------------------| | **Biological / Disease‑specific** | **Heterogeneous and immunosuppressive TME** – GBM contains spatially intermingled tumor, necrotic, hypoxic, and immune‑rich zones; immune cell phenotypes are plastic and differ between primary and recurrent disease. | Makes it difficult for a single imaging metric to capture the “immune status” that truly predicts response. | | | **Blood‑brain barrier (BBB) dynamics** – Variable permeability influences contrast‑agent delivery and PET tracer uptake. | Confounds quantification; a low signal may reflect poor delivery rather than low immune activity. | | | **Limited ground truth** – Serial biopsies are rarely feasible; post‑mortem tissue is scarce; peripheral blood does not reflect intracranial immunity. | Hinders rigorous correlation of imaging features with histology or functional assays. | | **Technical / Imaging** | **Standardization of acquisition** – Differences in scanner hardware (1.5 T vs 3 T vs 7 T), pulse sequences, contrast agents, PET tracers, and reconstruction algorithms. | Reduces reproducibility across sites and trials. | | | **Quantitative accuracy & calibration** – Radiomics/texture, kinetic modeling, and deep‑learning feature extraction are highly sensitive to noise, motion, and preprocessing pipelines. | Leads to “site‑specific signatures” that cannot be generalized. | | | **Lack of validated immune‑specific tracers** – Few PET ligands reliably bind to CD8⁺ T cells, PD‑L1, or activation markers in the brain (e.g., ^89Zr‑Df‑anti‑CD8, ^18F‑FET for metabolic activity). | Limits ability to directly image the immune component; most studies rely on surrogate metrics (e.g., perfusion, diffusion). | | **Data / Analytics** | **Small, non‑harmonized datasets** – Most studies are single‑center, <50 patients, with heterogeneous treatment regimens. | Inhibits robust machine‑learning model training and external validation. | | | **Over‑fitting & lack of interpretability** – Radiomic signatures often contain >100 features; many are not biologically interpretable. | Regulators and clinicians demand explainable biomarkers. | | | **Integration with other –omics** – Immune biomarkers are multi‑modal (genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, cytokines). Current pipelines rarely fuse imaging with these data. | Misses synergistic predictive power. | | **Regulatory / Clinical‑trial** | **No clear regulatory pathway** – FDA’s Biomarker Qualification Program (BQP) has examples mostly for blood‐based or histology biomarkers; imaging‑immune biomarkers in neuro‑oncology are virtually absent. | Uncertainty about evidentiary standards slows sponsor investment. | | | **Lack of prospective, adaptive trial designs** – Most immunotherapy trials in GBM still use fixed‑dose, non‑biomarker‑driven arms. | No real‑world data to demonstrate clinical utility. | | | **Reimbursement & health‑economics** – Payers need evidence that additional imaging (e.g., PET‑CT with a novel tracer) improves outcomes enough to offset cost. | Hinders adoption even after validation. | | **Operational / Logistical** | **Access to advanced scanners and tracers** – Small community hospitals lack 7 T MRI or on‑site cyclotron for short‑half‑life PET isotopes. | Limits broad implementation and generalizability. | | | **Training & workflow integration** – Radiologists, neuro‑oncologists, and trial teams need standardized reporting and decision‑support tools. | Without clear SOPs the biomarker remains academic. | --- ## 2. Step‑by‑Step Roadmap to Validation & Implementation ### Phase 0 – Conceptual Groundwork | Action | Details | |--------|---------| | **Define the clinical question** – e.g., “Can we identify GBM patients who will benefit from anti‑PD‑1 within 6 weeks of therapy?” | Drives selection of imaging modality & endpoint. | | **Form a multi‑disciplinary consortium** – Radiology, neuro‑oncology, immunology, medical physics, bioinformatics, regulatory affairs, patient advocacy. | Enables shared protocols, data‑sharing agreements, and joint funding (e.g., NIH‑NCI R01, European Horizon, industry partnerships). | | **Create a pre‑competitive repository** – Standardized imaging, clinical, and tissue data (e.g., “GBM‑Immune Imaging Hub”). | Facilitates external validation early on. | --- ### Phase I – Discovery & Technical Feasibility | Milestone | Tasks & Success Criteria | |-----------|--------------------------| | **Select imaging modality & immune tracer** | • MRI‑based (DSC, DCE, diffusion‑tensor, amide‑proton‑transfer, MR‑spectroscopy) **and/or** PET tracer (e.g., ^89Zr‑Df‑anti‑CD8, ^18F‑FDG, ^18F‑FET, ^89Zr‑αPD‑L1).
• Conduct phantom studies and test–retest reproducibility (CoV < 10 %). | | **Develop quantitative feature pipeline** | • Segmentation (semi‑automatic, AI‑assisted) of tumor & peritumoral edema.
• Extract radiomic, kinetic, and deep‑feature maps.
• Technical validation: intra‑observer, inter‑observer ICC > 0.80. | | **Generate pilot “ground‑truth”** | • In patients scheduled for surgical resection (baseline or recurrence), obtain spatially co‑registered tissue cores (image‑guided stereotactic biopsies).
• Perform multiplex immunofluorescence / CyTOF for CD8, CD4, T‑reg, macrophage M1/M2, PD‑L1, cytokines.
• Correlate imaging metrics with cellular densities (Spearman ρ > 0.6). | | **Proof‑of‑concept predictive model** | • Use cross‑validated (e.g., 5‑fold) machine‑learning (LASSO, random forest, GNN) to predict “immune‑hot” vs “immune‑cold” status.
• Report AUC ≥ 0.80 in internal test set. | --- ### Phase II – Multi‑Center Analytical Validation | Milestone | Tasks & Success Criteria | |-----------|--------------------------| | **Standardized acquisition protocol** | • Publish SOPs for MRI sequences (TR/TE, flip angle, voxel size) and PET tracer synthesis, dosing, uptake time.
• Implement site‑qualification using a digital reference object (DRO) and a traveling phantom. | | **Harmonization & Quality Control** | • Centralized image QC platform (e.g., XNAT + AI‑driven QC).
• Apply ComBat or deep‑learning harmonization to remove scanner effects. | | **External cohort testing** | • Enroll ≥150 GBM patients across 4‑6 academic centers, all receiving the same immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab + radiation).
• Blind external analysts to outcomes.
• Demonstrate reproducible performance: AUC ≥ 0.75, calibration slope 0.9‑1.1. | | **Robustness analyses** | • Subset analyses by MRI field strength, lesion location, MGMT methylation status, steroid use. | | **Pre‑regulatory engagement** | • Submit a **Letter of Intent (LOI)** to the FDA’s Biomarker Qualification Program (BQP) outlining the biomarker, its intended use, and supporting data. | --- ### Phase III – Clinical Qualification & Utility | Milestone | Tasks & Success Criteria | |-----------|--------------------------| | **Prospective, biomarker‑driven trial** | • Randomized phase II/III trial with two arms: (1) **Biomarker‑guided immunotherapy** (e.g., treat only immune‑hot lesions, or adapt dose based on early imaging), (2) **Standard of care**.
• Primary endpoint: progression‑free survival (PFS) or overall survival (OS) improvement ≥ 20 % in biomarker arm. | | **Co‑primary analytical endpoint** | • Demonstrate that the imaging biomarker is **predictive** (interaction test p < 0.05) and **prognostic** (hazard ratio < 1 for immune‑hot vs cold). | | **Health‑Economic model** | • Cost‑effectiveness analysis: incremental cost‑effectiveness ratio (ICER) < $100k/QALY when using imaging to select patients. | | **Regulatory qualification** | • Submit full **Biomarker Qualification Package** (BQPA) to FDA (or EMA). Includes: analytical validation, clinical validation, intended context of use (CofU), and evidence of clinical utility. | | **Guideline endorsement** | • Collaborate with NCCN, EANO, ASCO to incorporate the biomarker into treatment algorithms (e.g., “Consider anti‑PD‑1 in patients with IDIB‑defined immune‑hot GBM”). | --- ### Phase IV – Real‑World Implementation | Requirement | How to Achieve | |-------------|----------------| | **Reimbursement** | • Provide payer dossiers (outcome data, budget impact).
• Seek coverage decisions (e.g., CMS NTAP, private payer contracts). | | **Clinical workflow integration** | • Embed automated feature extraction into PACS/RIS (e.g., via DICOM‑RT or FHIR).
• Create a decision‑support report (“Immune‑Score = 0.78 (hot) → recommended anti‑PD‑1”). | | **Training & credentialing** | • Develop CME modules for radiologists & neuro‑oncologists.
• Offer site‑specific certification (e.g., “Certified GBM Immune Imaging Center”). | | **Ongoing performance monitoring** | • Establish a post‑market surveillance registry to track assay drift, new therapies, and long‑term outcomes. | | **Scalability** | • Validate simplified protocols (e.g., 1‑hour PET without arterial sampling) for community hospitals; explore **synthetic‑CT**/AI‑based attenuation correction to reduce need for CT. | --- ## 3. Putting It All Together – A “Blueprint” Timeline | Year | Key Activities | |------|----------------| | **0‑1** | Consortium formation, secure funding, define clinical question, develop SOPs, phantom & test‑retest studies. | | **1‑2** | Pilot biopsies + imaging, generate initial radiomic/AI models, submit BQP LOI. | | **2‑3** | Multi‑center analytical validation (≥150 pts), harmonization pipeline, external blind testing, refine model. | | **3‑5** | Launch biomarker‑driven phase II trial, collect survival & health‑econ data, submit full BQPA. | | **5‑6** | Regulatory qualification, guideline updates, payer negotiations, rollout of automated reporting software. | | **6+** | Nationwide implementation, registry for real‑world evidence, periodic re‑qualification as new immunotherapies emerge. | --- ## 4. Practical Checklist for a Team Starting the Journey | Category | Checklist Item | |----------|----------------| | **Scientific** | • Identify immune component(s) to image (CD8⁺ T cells, PD‑L1, myeloid activation).
• Confirm that the chosen tracer or MRI metric has pre‑clinical evidence of specificity in GBM models. | | **Technical** | • Standardize acquisition across all participating sites.
• Implement automated segmentation + QC pipeline. | | **Data** | • Build a secure, FAIR‑compliant database (imaging, pathology, genomics, clinical).
• Pre‑register analysis plan (to avoid p‑hacking). | | **Regulatory** | • Early engagement meetings with FDA/EMA (pre‑IND or Q‑Submission). | | **Operational** | • Secure access to cyclotron or commercial tracer supplier; arrange “just‑in‑time” production. | | **Financial** | • Budget for tracer synthesis, extra scan time, and central data coordination (~$2‑3 M for a multi‑center validation). | | **Patient** | • Develop consent language clarifying additional imaging and possible biopsy.
• Include patient advocates in protocol design. | --- ## 5. Key Take‑Home Messages 1. **Rigorous standardization** (hardware, acquisition, processing) is the single most critical hurdle; without it, any promising signal collapses when moving beyond a single site. 2. **Ground‑truth correlation** with spatially matched tissue is essential to prove that an imaging feature truly reflects immune activity—not just vascular permeability or edema. 3. **Regulatory clarity** can be accelerated by early, structured dialogue with the FDA’s Biomarker Qualification Program and by framing the biomarker as a **companion diagnostic** for a specific immunotherapy. 4. **Clinical utility must be demonstrated** in a prospective, biomarker‑guided trial—not merely retrospectively. The endpoint should be a hard clinical outcome (OS/PFS) and not just “change in immune score.” 5. **Implementation science matters**: reimbursement, workflow integration, and training are decisive for real‑world uptake, especially in community neuro‑oncology settings where most GBM patients receive care. By systematically addressing each barrier through the staged roadmap above, the field can move from exploratory radiomics papers toward **validated, regulatory‑qualified imaging immune biomarkers** that genuinely guide immunotherapy decisions for glioblastoma patients.
