Below is a **step‑by‑step playbook** for qualitative researchers who want to bring large language models (LLMs) (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, open‑source alternatives) into their projects **without sacrificing interpretive depth, transparency, or ethical rigor**. It is organized around three “pillars” that match the concerns you raised: | Pillar | Core Goal | Key Practices | Concrete Tools & Resources | |--------|-----------|----------------|-----------------------------| | **1️⃣ Interpretive Fidelity** | Keep the researcher’s analytic lens front‑and‑center. | • Use LLMs as *assistants*, not *analysts*.
• Maintain a *human‑in‑the‑loop* loop for every AI‑generated suggestion.
• Document every prompt, model version, and temperature setting. | Prompt‑logging notebooks (Jupyter, RMarkdown), Version‑controlled prompt repositories (GitHub), “Model‑cards” from the model provider. | | **2️⃣ Transparency & Reproducibility** | Make it possible for peers (and yourself) to trace exactly how AI contributed. | • Create a *Method‑Augmented Transparency Log* (MAT‑Log).
• Share the full *prompt–response* pairs alongside the final analytic output.
• Archive the exact model checkpoint (or a DOI if using a hosted API). | Open Science Framework (OSF) project, Zenodo deposits, “LLM‑audit” spreadsheets. | | **3️⃣ Ethical Safeguards** | Reduce bias, protect participants, and honor data‑privacy obligations. | • Conduct a *risk‑assessment matrix* before any AI use.
• Apply *data‑minimisation* and *pseudonymisation* before feeding text to the model.
• Perform *bias‑spotting* checks on AI‑generated suggestions.
• Obtain informed consent that explicitly mentions AI processing. | Data‑masking scripts (Python/regex), Institutional Review Board (IRB) addenda templates, Fairness‑evaluation libraries (e.g., Fairlearn, AI Fairness 360). | Below you’ll find **a practical workflow**, **checklists**, **sample prompts**, and **resources** to help you implement each pillar. --- ## 📚 QUICK‑START WORKFLOW (13‑Step Cycle) 1. **Define the Research Question & Analytic Frame** - Write a concise analytic memo (e.g., “We will conduct a grounded‑theory coding of interview transcripts to understand…”) and keep it visible throughout the project. 2. **Perform an Ethical & Risk Assessment** - Use the *AI‑Ethics Risk Matrix* (see Checklist A). - Decide: *Will any participant data be sent to a third‑party API?* If yes, document the data‑handling agreement and consider an on‑premise open‑source model instead. 3. **Select an Appropriate LLM** - **Hosted API** (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini): convenient, up‑to‑date, but data travel outside your firewall. - **Self‑hosted/open‑source** (LLaMA‑2, Mistral, Zephyr): full control, easier to comply with GDPR/IRB‑level data residency. - Record the model name, version, and provider in your MAT‑Log. 4. **Prepare the Data (De‑Identification + Chunking)** - Strip names, locations, IDs, and any “direct identifiers”. - Replace them with generic tokens (`[PERSON_1]`, `[ORG_X]`) that you keep in a **secure mapping file**. - Split long transcripts into 2‑4 k‑token chunks (most APIs have a context‑window limit). 5. **Create a Prompt Library** - Write *template prompts* for each analytic task (e.g., “Generate an initial list of themes from this 2 k‑token excerpt”). - Include **metadata fields**: `{{source_id}}`, `{{chunk_number}}`, `{{date}}`. - Store the templates in a version‑controlled folder (e.g., `prompts/grounded_theory.md`). 6. **Run a Pilot Batch (≤5 % of data)** - Send a small, representative sample to the LLM. - Capture the **prompt → response** in a CSV/JSON log (timestamp, temperature, max tokens, etc.). 7. **Human‑Centred Review & Reflexivity Check** - Researchers read the AI output **before** accepting or discarding it. - Use a *Reflexivity Grid* (see Checklist B) to note: “Did the LLM surface something I’d missed? Did it introduce terminology that feels foreign to the data?” 8. **Iterate Prompt & Parameter Settings** - Adjust temperature, top‑p, or add “system messages” that embed your analytic stance (e.g., “You are a sociologist trained in critical discourse analysis”). - Re‑run the pilot until you reach a *satisficing* level of usefulness (e.g., >70 % of AI‑suggested codes are retained after human review). 9. **Scale Up** - Apply the refined prompt to the full data set, **still logging each call**. - If you’re using a hosted API, set a rate‑limit and budget alerts to avoid runaway costs. 10. **Synthesize AI‑Generated Artifacts** - Export AI‑suggested codes, memos, or summaries into your qualitative software (NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, Dedoose). - Tag each imported artifact with a provenance label (`LLM‑v2‑temp0.3‑chunk‑12`). 11. **Critical Comparative Coding** - Perform *dual coding*: one set by the researcher alone, another set that incorporates AI suggestions. - Compute inter‑coder agreement (Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α) to quantify the impact of the AI aid. 12. **Document Transparency Artifacts** - Upload the **MAT‑Log**, prompt library, and a *model‑card* (including provider, date accessed, and any known limitations) to an open‑science repository (OSF, Zenodo). 13. **Reflect & Report** - In the methods section, explicitly state: - Why the LLM was chosen. - How data were de‑identified. - Which prompts were used and how they evolved. - The proportion of AI‑generated versus researcher‑generated codes. - Any bias‑mitigation steps taken. --- ## ✅ CHECKLIST A – AI‑ETHICS RISK MATRIX | Risk Area | Question | Decision Rule | |----------|----------|---------------| | **Data Privacy** | Will raw text be transmitted to a third‑party server? | **No** → use self‑hosted model or anonymise further. | | **Legal Compliance** | Does the data contain GDPR‑sensitive info (EU citizens)? | Must obtain explicit consent for AI processing or apply a “data‑processing addendum”. | | **Model Bias** | Is the model known to amplify gender, racial, or socioeconomic stereotypes? | If yes, add *bias‑mitigation prompts* (e.g., “Avoid assumptions about gender in this excerpt”). | | **Intellectual Property** | Do participants own the transcript content? | Include a clause in consent that **you may use** the text for “automated analysis”. | | **Cost & Sustainability** | Are API fees within the project budget? | Set per‑month caps; log expenses for transparency. | | **Reproducibility** | Can another scholar obtain the exact same model version? | Prefer models with stable release IDs (e.g., `llama-2-13b-chat-hf v2.1`). | --- ## ✅ CHECKLIST B – REFLEXIVITY GRID (Human Review of AI Output) | Dimension | Prompt | Example Entry | |-----------|--------|---------------| | **Surprise** | Did the AI suggest a theme that was not on my radar? | “AI flagged ‘digital fatigue’ – I had only been looking for ‘work‑life balance’. Might deserve deeper probing.” | | **Fit** | Does the wording echo participants’ own language? | “AI used ‘stressors’ whereas interviewees said ‘pressure points’. Keep original phrasing for authenticity.” | | **Bias Flag** | Does the suggestion reflect stereotypical assumptions? | “AI repeatedly coded ‘women’ as ‘emotional’, which mirrors known gender bias. Discard.” | | **Theoretical Alignment** | Does the AI output line up with my conceptual framework? | “AI’s ‘institutional inertia’ aligns with my structuralist lens – retain.” | | **Action** | What will you do with this suggestion? (keep, edit, discard) | “Edit – retain ‘digital fatigue’ but re‑code under ‘technology overload’.” | --- ## 🛠️ SAMPLE PROMPT TEMPLATES > **Tip:** Always start with a *system* message that defines the researcher’s perspective. This reduces “drift” and helps the model stay on task. ### 1️⃣ Initial Thematic Exploration ```text System: You are an experienced qualitative researcher specializing in grounded theory. Your role is to surface potential concepts from interview excerpts while preserving participants’ voice. User: Below is a 2,200‑token excerpt from interview #23 (pseudonymized). Identify **up to 8** candidate concepts that appear in the text. Provide each concept as a short phrase (max 4 words) and a one‑sentence justification taken **verbatim** from the excerpt (use [...] to indicate omitted parts). Do NOT infer beyond the data. Excerpt: [BEGIN EXCERPT] ... (insert cleaned text) ... [END EXCERPT] ``` **Parameters:** `temperature=0.3`, `max_tokens=500`, `top_p=0.9`. ### 2️⃣ Coding Assistance (based on existing codebook) ```text System: You will act as a coding assistant. Use the following codebook verbatim. If a passage does not fit any code, return "No code". Codebook: 1. Power dynamics – … 2. Resource scarcity – … 3. Emotional labor – … User: Apply the codebook to the following passage (pseudonymized). Return a JSON list of {segment: "...", code: "..."} objects. Passage: [BEGIN PASSAGE] ... [/END PASSAGE] ``` **Parameters:** `temperature=0.0` (deterministic), `max_tokens=300`. ### 3️⃣ Summarising a Cluster of Interviews ```text System: Summarise the key points while preserving nuance. question: How do nonlinear constraints such as apparent power (quadratic) or nodal voltage limits change the design and performance guarantees of online algorithms for allocating electrical demands compared to problems with only linear constraints?
model_answer:
## Overview  

When you move from a “nice” linear feasibility/optimization model to one that contains **non‑linear constraints** (e.g., apparent‑power limits \(|S_i|^2 = P_i^2+Q_i^2\le \bar S_i^2\) or quadratic voltage‑drop limits \(|V_j|^2\le \bar V_j^2\)), two things happen at the algorithmic level:

| Aspect | Linear‑only setting | With quadratic (or more general) constraints |
|--------|---------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Mathematical structure** | Feasible region is a polyhedron → separable, convex, and can be described by a matrix \(A\) and vector \(b\). | Feasible region is a **convex quadratically‑constrained set** (a second‑order cone, SOC) or, after linearisation, a *non‑convex* region if you keep the exact physics. |
| **Online decision rule** | Often a simple greedy or primal‑dual rule based on a linear feasibility test (`A·x ≤ b`). | Decision must test a **quadratic feasibility test** (e.g., \(x^\top Q x+ c^\top x \le d\)) or a conic projection, which is more expensive and may require an extra “safety margin”. |
| **Competitive‑ratio analysis** | The competitive ratio typically follows from linear packing/covering duality (e.g., \(1-1/e\) for online knapsack, constant‑factor bounds for online matching). | You must work with **dual cones** (SOC dual = SOC) and with *quadratic* dual variables. The analysis often incurs an extra \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) factor or logarithmic loss because you cannot separate the dimensions cleanly. |
| **Performance guarantees** | Exact feasibility can be guaranteed with *deterministic* or *randomized* algorithms; often you get **tight** constants. | Guarantees become **approximate** (e.g., “feasible up to a factor \((1+\epsilon)\)” or “within a 2‑approximation of the power‑budget”). The extra curvature forces you to conservatively shrink the admissible region, which reduces the attained objective. |
| **Implementation cost** | Simple linear‑program (LP) solves or even O(1) updates per request. | Requires solving a **second‑order cone program (SOCP)** or a small convex quadratic subproblem per arrival, which is more computationally intensive (though still polynomial‑time). |
| **Robustness to uncertainty** | Linear constraints are insensitive to small perturbations; error bounds are additive. | Quadratic constraints amplify errors (e.g., a small over‑estimate of current \(I\) creates a quadratic error in apparent power), so the algorithm must incorporate *margin* or *robust* designs. |

Below we unpack the **why** behind each entry, then sketch how the design of an online algorithm changes in practice, and finally list the *most common* performance‑guarantee results that appear in the literature.

---

## 1️⃣  From Linear to Quadratic Feasibility

### 1.1 Linear packing/covering (baseline)

A classic online packing problem can be written as  

\[
\max \sum_{t=1}^{T} v_t \, x_t \quad
\text{s.t. } \sum_{t=1}^{T} a_t x_t \le b,\;\; x_t\in\{0,1\},
\]

where each request \(t\) arrives with a weight \(v_t\) and a resource‑usage vector \(a_t\in\mathbb R_+^m\). The feasible set is a **polyhedron**. Online primal‑dual algorithms keep a dual vector \(y\) and accept request \(t\) if  

\[
a_t^\top y \le \alpha v_t,
\]

for a pre‑chosen \(\alpha\). The analysis reduces to a simple **potential‑function** argument that yields a constant competitive ratio (e.g., \(\frac{1}{2}\) for the classic online knapsack, \((1-1/e)\) for the fractional version).

### 1.2 Second‑order‑cone (SOC) constraints

Apparent‑power constraints are of the form  

\[
P_i^2 + Q_i^2 \le \bar S_i^2, \qquad (P_i,Q_i) \in \mathbb R^2,
\]

or, in vector form,  

\[
\|(P_i,Q_i)\|_2 \le \bar S_i.
\]

A set of such constraints for many devices forms an **intersection of SOCs**:

\[
\mathcal{K}= \{ x\mid \|A_j x + b_j\|_2 \le c_j^\top x + d_j,\; j=1,\dots,m\}.
\]

Key properties:

| Property | Linear | SOC |
|----------|--------|-----|
| Convex | Yes (polyhedron) | Yes (convex cone) |
| Closed form projection | Simple truncation onto a half‑space | Requires solving a small QP (a projection onto an SOC is O(dim)) |
| Dual cone | Same half‑space | Same SOC (self‑dual) |
| Separation oracle | Dot‑product > b? | Norm inequality > …? (more expensive) |

The *self‑duality* of SOCs is a blessing because primal‑dual analysis still works, but the **norm** introduces a \(\sqrt{\;\cdot\;}\) nonlinearity that prevents you from splitting the contribution of each request into independent coordinates. In practice you have to bound the norm **jointly** across all dimensions.

---

## 2️⃣  Design Changes in the Online Algorithm  

### 2.1 General recipe (linear → SOC)

| Step (linear) | SOC adaptation |
|---------------|----------------|
| **(a) Maintain a dual price vector** \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\). | **(a')** Maintain a dual *conic* price vector \(y\) that lives in the **dual SOC**. This means each component is a scalar plus a *direction* (a vector of length equal to the SOC dimension). |
| **(b) Acceptance test**: check if \(a_t^\top y \le v_t\). | **(b')** Acceptance test becomes \(\|A_t^\top y + \beta_t\|_2 \le v_t\) for some appropriately defined matrices \(A_t\) that map the request onto each cone. Often you linearise the norm with a *support‑function* bound: \(\|z\|_2 \le \lambda \iff z^\top u \le \lambda\) for all \(\|u\|_2\le 1\). In an online algorithm you pick a **worst‑case direction** (e.g., the current most‑loaded line) and test a linear inequality derived from it. |
| **(c) Dual update**: increase \(y\) proportionally to \(a_t\) when a request is accepted. | **(c')** Increase the *SOC‑dual* vector along the direction of the request: \(y \gets y + \eta\, (A_t^\top u + \beta_t)\) where \(u\) is the unit vector that **maximises** the left‑hand side of the SOC constraint. This is essentially a **subgradient step** on the norm. |
| **(d) Feasibility proof**: use linear feasibility ⇒ simple counting argument. | **(d')** Use the **conic version of weak duality**: \(\sum_t v_t x_t \le y^\top b\) holds if \(y\) lies in the dual cone. You need to show that the accumulated dual cost stays bounded **relative to** the budget \(b\). Because of the norm, you often incur an extra factor \(\sqrt{m}\) or \(\log m\) when you sum across cones. |

#### Concrete example: online allocation with apparent‑power limits

Suppose a distribution feeder has \(L\) lines. For line \(\ell\) the apparent‑power budget is \(\bar S_\ell\). Request \(t\) draws a complex power vector \((P_{t\ell},Q_{t\ell})\) on each line it traverses (the vector may be zero on lines not in its path).  

**Linear model (approximation)** – you would replace the SOC by two linear constraints  

\[
\sum_{t} P_{t\ell}x_t \le \bar S_\ell,\qquad 
\sum_{t} Q_{t\ell}x_t \le \bar S_\ell,
\]

and run a standard primal‑dual algorithm. This is **pessimistic** because the actual feasible set is larger (the circle contains the square).

**SOC‑aware online algorithm** – keep a dual scalar \(y_\ell\) *and* a dual direction vector \(z_\ell\in\mathbb R^2\). When request \(t\) arrives you compute  

\[
\alpha_{t\ell}= y_\ell\,\bar S_\ell + z_\ell^\top (P_{t\ell},Q_{t\ell}),
\]

and accept if \(\sum_\ell \alpha_{t\ell} \le v_t\). After acceptance you update  

\[
y_\ell \gets y_\ell + \eta\,\frac{\bar S_\ell}{\|(P_{t\ell},Q_{t\ell})\|_2},\qquad

|---------|------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|

\[

| Property | Linear | SOC |
|----------|--------|-----|

question: What are the main limitations, potential risks, and clinical pitfalls of using an AI-based system to screen for pulmonary embolism on non-contrast chest CT images before confirmatory testing?
model_answer:
## Overview  

Artificial‑intelligence (AI) algorithms—most often deep‑learning convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or hybrid radiomics‑AI models—are increasingly being deployed to **pre‑screen** non‑contrast chest CT (NC‑CT) examinations for signs of **pulmonary embolism (PE)** before a dedicated contrast‑enhanced CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is ordered.  
While the concept is attractive (earlier flagging of high‑risk patients, reduction of missed diagnoses, workflow triage), the technology is still embryonic and comes with a suite of **limitations, risks, and clinical pitfalls** that must be understood before it is integrated into routine practice.

Below is a concise but comprehensive synthesis of the **major issues** that radiologists, clinicians, and hospital administrators should consider.

---

## 1. Technical & Performance Limitations  

| Category | Why it matters | Typical impact on PE screening |
|----------|----------------|-------------------------------|
| **Training data bias** | Datasets often derived from a single institution, scanner brand, or patient population (e.g., mostly oncologic scans). | Poor generalisation to community hospitals, pediatric populations, or scanners with different reconstruction kernels. |
| **Limited ground‑truth labels** | In NC‑CT, “PE” is usually inferred from a later CTPA, not directly visible. Labels can be noisy or incomplete. | False‑positive “PE” flags when the algorithm learns surrogate features (e.g., pleural effusion, lung consolidation) rather than true emboli. |
| **Resolution & slice thickness** | Non‑contrast chest CT is frequently performed at 5 mm thickness for lung cancer screening, whereas PE detection usually needs ≤1.5 mm. | Small subsegmental emboli are invisible on the source image, so the AI cannot magically “see” them; it may over‑call artifacts. |
| **Absence of intravascular contrast** | PE is a *vascular* pathology; in NC‑CT the vessels are isodense with surrounding parenchyma. | AI must rely on indirect signs (e.g., lung infarction, pleural‑based wedge‑shaped opacities) that are neither specific nor sensitive. |
| **Class imbalance** | True PE cases in NC‑CT datasets are rare (<1 %); models can achieve high AUC by simply predicting “no PE.” | Reported performance metrics (AUC > 0.9) may be misleading; sensitivity at clinically relevant thresholds can be <50 %. |
| **Explainability** | Most CNNs are “black boxes.” | Clinicians cannot verify *why* the model flagged an exam, making trust and error detection difficult. |
| **Model drift** | Scanner upgrades, new reconstruction algorithms, or changes in acquisition protocols can degrade performance over time. | Ongoing recalibration is required; otherwise, missed PE rates may rise unnoticed. |

---

## 2. Clinical Risks  

| Risk | Mechanism | Potential Consequence |
|------|-----------|-----------------------|
| **False‑negative screening** | Model fails to flag a true PE (e.g., subtle infarct, atypical presentation). | Delayed CTPA → missed or late treatment → increased morbidity/mortality. |
| **False‑positive screening** | Model flags a non‑PE finding (e.g., pneumonia, pulmonary edema) as embolic. | Unnecessary CTPA → radiation, contrast‑induced nephropathy (CIN), allergic reaction, cost, patient anxiety. |
| **Over‑reliance / automation bias** | Clinicians may accept AI output uncritically, especially in high‑throughput settings. | Systemic under‑ or over‑investigation, erosion of radiologist vigilance. |
| **Diagnostic anchoring** | An AI flag may bias downstream interpretation of the CTPA (e.g., “look for clot”). | Missed alternative diagnoses (e.g., aortic dissection, tumor) that could be clinically critical. |
| **Workflow bottlenecks** | If the AI generates many “positive” alerts, downstream imaging resources (CTPA slots, contrast media) can become scarce. | Delays for genuine high‑risk patients, increased wait times. |
| **Equity & disparity** | Training data under‑represent certain ethnic groups, ages, or body‑habitus. | Systematic under‑detection in those sub‑populations, widening health disparities. |
| **Legal & regulatory exposure** | Mis‑diagnosis attributable to AI can lead to malpractice claims. | Institutions may face liability even if the algorithm was only “decision support.” |

---

## 3. Clinical Pitfalls & Misinterpretations  

1. **Mistaking indirect signs for emboli**  
   - AI often learns to associate **wedge‑shaped peripheral opacities**, **pleural‑based ground‑glass**, or **pleural effusion** with PE.  
   - These findings are **nonspecific** (e.g., infection, infarction, pulmonary hemorrhage) and may be present without emboli.

2. **Ignoring the “negative predictive value” (NPV) myth**  
   - A high NPV in a low‑prevalence test does **not** guarantee safety when applied to a higher‑risk cohort (e.g., ICU patients).  
   - When prevalence rises, the absolute number of false negatives can become clinically unacceptable.

3. **Using AI as a “stand‑alone” rule-out tool**  
   - No current AI has achieved **≥ 95 % sensitivity** on NC‑CT; guidelines still mandate a **clinical pre‑test probability assessment** (e.g., Wells, Geneva) and, when indicated, a contrast study.

4. **Failure to incorporate clinical context**  
   - AI sees only the image; it cannot weigh D‑dimer, oxygen saturation, or recent surgery.  
   - A “negative” AI on a high‑risk patient (e.g., massive DVT) should **not** preclude further work‑up.

5. **Assuming AI can replace radiologist “second look”**  
   - Radiologists still need to verify that flagged regions correspond to true abnormality, especially given the high rate of artifacts (e.g., motion, beam hardening).

6. **Inadequate handling of incidental findings**  
   - AI may miss or misclassify **pulmonary nodules**, **coronary calcium**, or **aortic pathology** that are clinically important, shifting focus solely to PE.

---

## 4. Operational & Implementation Caveats  

| Issue | Detail | Mitigation |
|-------|--------|------------|
| **Integration into PACS/RIS** | Real‑time flagging requires seamless DICOM routing and alerting mechanisms. | Pilot in staging environment; use “soft‑alert” (e.g., icon) rather than forced workflow interruption. |
| **Threshold selection** | Trade‑off between sensitivity & specificity; threshold may be set differently for “triage” vs “screening.” | Establish **multiple operating points** (high‑sensitivity for emergent cases; high‑specificity for routine triage). |
| **Performance monitoring** | Continuous audit of false‑positive/negative rates. | Implement a **dashboard** with per‑site, per‑scanner, and per‑patient‑cohort metrics; schedule periodic re‑training. |
| **User education** | Radiologists and clinicians need to understand AI limitations. | Formal training sessions, “cheat‑sheet” of common pitfalls, and mandatory sign‑off that AI was reviewed. |
| **Regulatory compliance** | FDA/EMA clearance may be limited to specific indications (e.g., “detect PE on contrast CT”). | Verify that the intended use statement matches the deployment scenario; seek an **ex‑off‑label** use justification if necessary. |
| **Data privacy & security** | Cloud‑based inference can expose PHI. | Use on‑premise inference engines or encrypted transfer; adhere to HIPAA/GDPR. |

---

## 5. Practical Recommendations for Safe Use  

1. **Treat AI as a *triage aide*, not a diagnostic arbiter.**  
   - Flagged NC‑CTs should be **reviewed promptly** by a radiologist who decides whether a CTPA is warranted.

2. **Combine AI output with a validated clinical decision rule** (Wells, YEARS, PERC).  
   - Only when both AI and the clinical rule suggest low probability should a CTPA be omitted.

3. **Maintain a low threshold for CTPA in high‑risk contexts** (e.g., postoperative, cancer, immobilisation) regardless of AI output.

4. **Implement a “human‑in‑the‑loop” audit**: every AI‑positive case must be double‑checked; a random sample of AI‑negative cases should also be reviewed periodically.

5. **Document the AI call in the radiology report** (e.g., “AI algorithm detected possible pulmonary embolic changes; subsequent CTPA recommended”).  
   - This creates a clear chain‑of‑responsibility and aids future quality‑improvement analysis.

6. **Plan for periodic re‑training** using locally collected NC‑CT + CTPA pairs, especially after any major scanner or protocol change.

7. **Educate non‑radiology clinicians** about the algorithm’s performance limits; avoid “AI‑only” referrals.

---

## 6. Bottom‑Line Summary  

| Aspect | Key Take‑away |
|-------|---------------|
| **Technical feasibility** | AI can recognize *indirect* signs of PE on NC‑CT, but its **sensitivity** is limited (generally 40‑70 %) and **specificity** varies widely. |
| **Major risk** | Missed PE (false‑negative) and unnecessary CTPA (false‑positive) – both have real patient safety, cost, and legal implications. |
| **Clinical pitfall** | Over‑reliance on AI without integrating clinical probability leads to diagnostic anchoring and potential undertreatment. |
| **Implementation** | Must be coupled with robust quality‑control, continuous monitoring, and clear policies that keep a radiologist in the decision loop. |
| **Regulatory/ethical** | Ensure the AI’s cleared indication matches the use case; monitor for bias and equity impacts. |
| **Best practice** | Use as an **early‐warning/triage** tool, not a definitive rule‑out; confirm any positive AI flag with contrast‑enhanced CTPA, and never withhold CTPA when clinical suspicion is high despite a negative AI call. |

By acknowledging these constraints and instituting safeguards, health systems can **leverage the speed and consistency of AI** while preserving the accuracy, safety, and judgment that remain essential in pulmonary embolism diagnosis.

question: How do precise measurements of rare B meson decays to muon pairs test the Standard Model and constrain possible beyond–Standard-Model theories?
model_answer:
## Overview  

Rare decays of neutral \(B\) mesons into a pair of muons  

\[
B_s^0 \;\to\; \mu^+\mu^-, \qquad 
B_d^0 \;\to\; \mu^+\mu^-,
\]

are among the cleanest laboratories for probing the flavour sector of the Standard Model (SM) and for hunting signs of physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Their extraordinary theoretical cleanliness (tiny hadronic uncertainties) and their extreme suppression in the SM (branching fractions of order \(10^{-9}\)–\(10^{-10}\)) mean that any deviation—however small—in the measured rates, angular distributions, or CP‑violating observables would immediately point to new particles or interactions.

Below is a step‑by‑step exposition of **why** these decays are so powerful, **what the SM predicts**, **how the measurements are performed**, and **how the results translate into quantitative limits on BSM scenarios**. The discussion is organized into five parts:

1. **The SM picture** – effective Hamiltonian, loop (penguin/box) diagrams, helicity suppression, and the predicted branching fractions.  
2. **Experimental strategy** – how LHCb, CMS, ATLAS, and future experiments isolate the signal and control systematics.  
3. **Key observables** – branching ratios, effective lifetimes, and the ratio \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)/\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)\).  
4. **Interpretation in the language of Wilson coefficients** – mapping measurements onto the coefficients \(C_{10}, C_{S}, C_{P}\) (and their primed counterparts).  
5. **Constraints on BSM models** – supersymmetry, two‑Higgs‑doublet models, leptoquarks, Z′ bosons, and model‑independent effective‑field‑theory (SMEFT) bounds.

Each section includes the essential formulas, the current experimental numbers (as of 2024), and a “quick‑look” table that translates a typical deviation into a BSM scale.

---

## 1. The Standard‑Model Prediction  

### 1.1 Effective Hamiltonian for \(b\!\to\!s\ell^+\ell^-\)

At energies below the electroweak scale the flavour‑changing neutral‑current (FCNC) transition \(b\to s\ell^+\ell^-\) is described by an effective weak Hamiltonian

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}= -\frac{4 G_F}{\sqrt2}\,
\frac{\alpha_{\rm em}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
\sum_i \bigl(C_i(\mu) \, \mathcal O_i(\mu) + C_i'(\mu)\,\mathcal O_i'(\mu)\bigr) .
\]

For the purely leptonic decay the relevant operators are

| Operator | Definition | SM Wilson coefficient |
|----------|------------|-----------------------|
| \(\mathcal O_{10}\) | \((\bar s \gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\ell \gamma^\mu \gamma_5 \ell)\) | \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.31\) |
| \(\mathcal O_{S}\)   | \((\bar s P_R b)(\bar\ell \ell)\) | 0 (tiny, \(\propto m_\ell m_b / M_W^2\)) |
| \(\mathcal O_{P}\)   | \((\bar s P_R b)(\bar\ell \gamma_5 \ell)\) | 0 (tiny, \(\propto m_\ell m_b / M_W^2\)) |

\(P_{L,R}=(1\mp\gamma_5)/2\). In the SM the scalar and pseudoscalar operators are essentially absent; the decay is driven almost exclusively by \(\mathcal O_{10}\).

### 1.2 Loop‑induced amplitude  

The amplitude comes from two classes of diagrams:

1. **Electroweak box** diagrams with a \(W\) and a top quark.  
2. **\(Z\)-penguin** diagrams (the dominant piece).  

Both are *one‑loop* processes, which explains the \(10^{-9}\)–\(10^{-10}\) suppression. In addition there is **helicity suppression**: the final‑state muons must have opposite helicities to couple to the axial‑vector current, giving a factor \(\propto m_\mu^2\).

### 1.3 Branching‑fraction formula  

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal B(B_q^0\!\to\! \mu^+\mu^-)=
\frac{G_F^2 \alpha_{\rm em}^2}{16\pi^3}
\,\tau_{B_q}\,f_{B_q}^2\,M_{B_q}\,
|V_{tb}V_{tq}^*|^2\,
\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{M_{B_q}^2}}\,
\Bigl|C_{10}^{\rm SM}\Bigr|^2\, .
}
\]

All hadronic physics is encoded in the decay constant \(f_{B_q}\), known from lattice QCD with sub‑percent precision. Numerically (2023 lattice averages):

| Decay | SM prediction (incl. \(\Delta\Gamma_s\) effects) |
|-------|-----------------------------------------------|
| \(B_s^0\to\mu^+\mu^-\) | \((3.66 \pm 0.14)\times10^{-9}\) |
| \(B_d^0\to\mu^+\mu^-\) | \((1.06 \pm 0.04)\times10^{-10}\) |

The uncertainties are dominated by CKM elements and \(f_{B_q}\); the perturbative part (the Wilson coefficient) is known to better than 1 % (including NNLO QCD + NLO electroweak).

---

## 2. Experimental Determination  

### 2.1 General features  

* **Very low yields**: Even with the enormous \(b\bar b\) production at the LHC (∼\(10^{12}\) \(B\) mesons per fb\(^{-1}\)), one expects only a few hundred \(B_s\!\to\!\mu^+\mu^-\) events per 10 fb\(^{-1}\).  
* **Backgrounds**: Dominated by combinatorial dimuon pairs from semileptonic decays and partially reconstructed \(B\) decays (e.g. \(B\to h\mu\nu\) with a hadron mis‑identified as a muon).  
* **Key experimental handles**: precise muon momentum measurement, excellent vertex resolution (to separate the displaced decay vertex), and particle‑identification (muon vs. pion/kaon).

### 2.2 Analyses at the LHC  

| Experiment | Integrated luminosity (2022) | Signal‑to‑background (S/B) | Measured \(\mathcal B\) |
|------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------|
| LHCb (Run 1+2) | 9 fb\(^{-1}\) | ∼ 5 | \((3.09^{+0.46}_{-0.43})\times10^{-9}\) |
| CMS (Run 1+2) | 140 fb\(^{-1}\) | ∼ 1 | \((3.83^{+0.38}_{-0.36})\times10^{-9}\) |
| ATLAS (Run 2) | 140 fb\(^{-1}\) | ∼ 0.5 | \((2.8\pm0.7)\times10^{-9}\) |
| **Combination (LHC‑Run 2)** | – | – | \((3.10\pm0.22)\times10^{-9}\) |

The combination is compatible with the SM at the 1.3 σ level. For the even rarer \(B_d\) channel only an upper limit exists:

\[
\mathcal B(B_d\!\to\!\mu^+\mu^-) < 1.1\times10^{-10}\;(95\%~\text{CL}) .
\]

### 2.3 Future prospects  

| Facility | Target integrated luminosity | Expected statistical precision ( \(\mathcal B(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) ) |
|----------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| LHCb Upgrade II (2035) | 300 fb\(^{-1}\) | 3 % (≈ \(0.1\times10^{-9}\) absolute) |
| High‑Luminosity LHC (CMS/ATLAS) | 3000 fb\(^{-1}\) | 2–3 % (systematics dominate) |
| FCC‑hh (100 TeV) | ∼ 10 ab\(^{-1}\) | < 1 % (theoretical error becomes limiting) |
| Belle II (Super‑KEKB) | 50 ab\(^{-1}\) | 10 % (statistically limited, but complementary for \(B_d\)) |

The ultimate precision will be limited by the lattice‑QCD inputs and by the CKM element \(|V_{ts}|\); these are expected to improve to the sub‑percent level within the next decade.

---

## 3. Observables that Test the SM  

| Observable | SM expectation | What BSM can do |
|------------|----------------|-----------------|

\[

+ C_{S}\,\langle\mathcal O_{S}\rangle
+ C_{P}\,\langle\mathcal O_{P}\rangle

&\times
\Bigl\{
\bigl| C_{10}^{\rm SM}+ C_{10}^{\rm NP}\bigr|^2
+ \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{4 m_\mu^2}\,
\bigl[ |C_{S} - C_{S}'|^2
      + |C_{P} - C_{P}' + 2 C_{10}^{\rm SM} \frac{m_\mu}{M_{B_q}}|^2 \bigr]
\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

=

\frac{1 + \mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma} y_s}
{1 - y_s^2},

=
\frac{|P|^2 - |S|^2}
{|P|^2 + |S|^2},
\]

\[
P \equiv C_{10}^{\rm SM}+ C_{10}^{\rm NP} + \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2 m_\mu}\,(C_{P} - C_{P}'), \qquad
S \equiv \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2 m_\mu}\,(C_{S} - C_{S}').
\]

In the SM, \(S\approx0\) and \(\mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma}\approx+1\), giving \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\approx\tau_{B_s}^{\rm L}\) (the lifetime of the light eigenstate). Any non‑zero \(S\) drives \(\mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma}\) toward \(-1\), making the measured lifetime approach the heavy‑state lifetime (\(\approx1.78\) ps). ## 5. Translating the Data into BSM Limits  

### 5.1 Model‑independent (Effective‑Field‑Theory) bounds

| Coefficient | Allowed interval (real) |
|------------|--------------------------|
| \(C_{10}^{\rm NP}\) | \([-0.18,\,0.12]\) |
| \(C_{S}\)          | \([-0.018,\,0.018]\) |
| \(C_{P}\)          | \([-0.012,\,0.012]\) |
| \(C_{10}'\)        | \([-0.05,\,0.05]\) |
| \(C_{S}'\)         | \([-0.02,\,0.02]\) |
| \(C_{P}'\)         | \([-0.02,\,0.02]\) |

\[

\frac{\tan^3\beta}{(1+\epsilon_0\tan\beta)}\,
\frac{m_t^2}{M_A^2}\,

\]

\[

\left(\frac{|\mu A_t|}{M_{\rm SUSY}^2}\right)^{1/2},
\]

---

  * Vector leptoquarks that explain the \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) anomalies are forced into the multi‑TeV regime unless their flavor couplings are highly hierarchical.

2. **Experimental strategy** – how LHCb, CMS, ATLAS, and future experiments isolate the signal and control systematics.  
3. **Key observables** – branching ratios, effective lifetimes, and the ratio \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)/\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)\).

## 1. The Standard‑Model Prediction  

### 1.1 Effective Hamiltonian for \(b\!\to\!s\ell^+\ell^-\)

\[

\frac{\alpha_{\rm em}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
\sum_i \bigl(C_i(\mu) \, \mathcal O_i(\mu) + C_i'(\mu)\,\mathcal O_i'(\mu)\bigr) .
\]

For the purely leptonic decay the relevant operators are

| Operator | Definition | SM Wilson coefficient |
|----------|------------|-----------------------|
| \(\mathcal O_{10}\) | \((\bar s \gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\ell \gamma^\mu \gamma_5 \ell)\) | \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.31\) |
| \(\mathcal O_{S}\)   | \((\bar s P_R b)(\bar\ell \ell)\) | 0 (tiny, \(\propto m_\ell m_b / M_W^2\)) |
| \(\mathcal O_{P}\)   | \((\bar s P_R b)(\bar\ell \gamma_5 \ell)\) | 0 (tiny, \(\propto m_\ell m_b / M_W^2\)) |

The amplitude comes from two classes of diagrams:

1. **Electroweak box** diagrams with a \(W\) and a top quark.  
2. **\(Z\)-penguin** diagrams (the dominant piece).

\[

\frac{G_F^2 \alpha_{\rm em}^2}{16\pi^3}

\Bigl|C_{10}^{\rm SM}\Bigr|^2\, .

\]

|-------|-----------------------------------------------|
| \(B_s^0\to\mu^+\mu^-\) | \((3.66 \pm 0.14)\times10^{-9}\) |
| \(B_d^0\to\mu^+\mu^-\) | \((1.06 \pm 0.04)\times10^{-10}\) |

question: How do Mg and Ti dopants typically affect the crystal structure, band gap (direct vs indirect), and electrical/optical properties of ZnO, and what physical mechanisms control those changes?

**Short answer**  
- **Mg‑doping** (Mg²⁺ → Zn²⁺) contracts the lattice, widens the band gap (still **direct** Γ→Γ), raises the conduction‑band minimum (CBM), reduces free‑carrier concentration (unless co‑doped) and makes ZnO more transparent in the UV‑visible region.  
- **Ti‑doping** (Ti⁴⁺ → Zn²⁺) expands the lattice a little, introduces *localized* d‑states that can turn the gap **indirect** (Γ→M or Γ→L) or create deep sub‑band‑gap levels, greatly increases n‑type conductivity (high donor concentration) but also generates strong sub‑band‑gap absorption (colored or “greenish” Ti‑ZnO).  

Both effects are governed by a handful of well‑established physical mechanisms:

| Mechanism | What it does | How it manifests for Mg | How it manifests for Ti |
|-----------|--------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Ionic‑size (strain) effect** | Substituting ion of different radius changes lattice parameters → modifies bond lengths & crystal field splitting | Mg²⁺ (0.72 Å) is **smaller** than Zn²⁺ (0.74 Å) → **compressive strain**, reduced a‑ and c‑axis, slight increase in Zn–O bond covalency | Ti⁴⁺ (0.61 Å in octahedral, ≈0.68 Å tetrahedral) is **similar‑to‑slightly smaller** than Zn²⁺, but the higher charge leads to a **local expansion** of the O‑tetrahedron to accommodate the extra electrons; net effect is a modest **lattice expansion** for low‑x (x ≈ 0.01‑0.05) and a turn‑over to contraction at higher x due to Mg‑like behaviour in mixed Mg/Ti alloys. |
| **Electronic‑structure (band‑edge) effect** | Change in the cation‑anion hybridisation shifts CBM and VBM. | Mg 3s states lie **higher** in energy than Zn 4s → the CBM moves up → **band‑gap widening** (≈ 30–50 meV per 1 % Mg). VBM is barely affected → gap remains **direct** (Γ→Γ). | Ti 3d⁰ (or 3d¹ after reduction) produce **Ti‑3d‑O‑2p hybrid states** that sit **below** the Zn‑derived CBM. At low Ti concentrations they act as **shallow donors**, pulling the CBM down (gap narrowing) or creating an *intermediate* sub‑band. At higher concentrations the Ti‑derived d‑band hybridises with the Zn‑derived conduction band, giving an **indirect gap** (Γ→M/L) and a **U‑shaped** conduction band. |
| **Charge‑compensation / defect chemistry** | The dopant’s valence vs host forces the formation of intrinsic defects (V_Zn, V_O, interstitials) that control carrier type and concentration. | Mg²⁺ is **isovalent** → does **not** create free carriers directly. However, strain can **suppress** native donors (V_O) → lower n‑type background → higher resistivity unless co‑doped (e.g., Al, Ga). | Ti⁴⁺ is **four‑valent**, two extra positive charges per substitution → each Ti creates **two electrons** that must be charge‑balanced. The easiest route is to generate **oxygen vacancies (V_O�⁺⁺)** or to occupy Ti⁴⁺ as Ti³⁺ (donor level). Result: **high n‑type conductivity** (10¹⁸‑10²⁰ cm⁻³). The excess electrons also screen the lattice, reducing the piezo‑electric response. |
| **Polaronic / localization effect** | d‑electrons can become trapped (small polarons) or form impurity bands. | Mg has no d‑electrons → no polaron formation. | Ti‑3d electrons are prone to **small‑polaron formation** especially when Ti is reduced (Ti³⁺). This leads to **temperature‑activated hopping conduction** and characteristic **mid‑infrared absorption** (~0.5–1 eV). |
| **Excitonic & optical transition changes** | Shift of exciton binding energy, appearance of new optical absorption. | Band‑gap widening pushes the **free‑exciton** energy higher, but the exciton binding energy (≈ 60 meV in ZnO) is only modestly changed. Result: **transparent UV window** up to ≈ 3.6‑4.0 eV for 5–10 % Mg. | Ti‑related d‑levels generate **sub‑band‑gap absorption** (often a broad band at 1.5‑2.5 eV) and can **quench** the near‑band‑edge excitonic peak. In heavily Ti‑doped films the material appears **yellow/green** because of Ti‑O charge‑transfer transitions. |
| **Piezo‑electric / ferroelectric coupling** | Strain and polarisation affect carrier mobility. | Compressive strain from Mg **enhances** the piezo‑electric coefficient c₃₃, slightly **increasing mobility** for carriers parallel to c‑axis. | The large local electric fields around Ti⁴⁺/Ti³⁺ clusters can **screen** the spontaneous polarization, reducing the effective piezo‑electric constants and creating internal fields that trap carriers. |

Below is a more detailed, step‑by‑step explanation of each point, together with the **key experimental signatures** and **theoretical models** that are commonly used to interpret them.

---

## 1. Crystal‑structure modifications

### 1.1 Wurtzite ZnO basics
- Space group **P6₃mc**, lattice parameters: *a* ≈ 3.25 Å, *c* ≈ 5.20 Å, Zn–O bond length ≈ 1.97 Å.
- Zn is tetrahedrally coordinated by O (sp³‑like hybridisation).

### 1.2 Mg‑substitution (Zn₁₋ₓMgₓO)
- **Ionic radius**: Mg²⁺ (tetrahedral) = 0.72 Å vs Zn²⁺ = 0.74 Å → 2–3 % size reduction per 10 % Mg.
- **XRD result**: systematic shift of (002), (101), (102) peaks to higher 2θ; linear decrease of *a* and *c* (Vegard’s law) up to the solubility limit (~30–35 % Mg for bulk, 50 % for thin films under strain).
- **Phase stability**: beyond the solubility limit a **rock‑salt MgO‑type** phase appears; the wurtzite‑to‑rock‑salt transformation is first‑order and is accompanied by loss of the direct gap.

### 1.3 Ti‑substitution (Zn₁₋ₓTiₓO)
- **Ionic radius**: Ti⁴⁺ (tetrahedral) ≈ 0.68 Å, Ti³⁺ ≈ 0.81 Å (if reduced). The formal charge drives **local lattice relaxation** that can be either *expansive* (if Ti³⁺) or *contractive* (if Ti⁴⁺). Experimental XRD shows a **slight expansion** of *c* (≤ 0.3 %) for x ≤ 0.05, then a trend toward *a* reduction at higher x, indicating a mix of strain states.
- **Secondary phases**: TiO₂ (anatase/rutile) or Ti₂O₃ start to appear for x > 0.1 unless growth is highly controlled (e.g., pulsed laser deposition at low oxygen pressure).

---

## 2. Band‑gap evolution

| Doping | Typical band‑gap change (ΔE_g) | Direct/Indirect? | Dominant cause |
|--------|------------------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Mg (0 → 10 %) | +0.3 → +0.5 eV (from 3.30 eV to ≈3.8 eV) | **Direct** (Γ→Γ) | Higher‑energy Mg‑4s CB contribution, lattice contraction (increased Zn‑O overlap) |
| Ti (0 → 5 %) | –0.05 → –0.15 eV (gap narrows) *or* indirect transition appears | Often **indirect** (Γ→M/L) if Ti > 2 % | Ti‑3d states hybridising with Zn‑4s, formation of impurity band; also strain‑induced band‑edge splitting |

### 2.1 Mg‑induced widening

- **k·p / empirical pseudopotential calculations** predict ΔE_g ≈ 0.04 eV per 1 % Mg for a fully relaxed lattice.
- The **conduction‑band curvature** becomes slightly larger (effective mass m*ₑ decreases from ≈ 0.24 m₀ to ≈ 0.20 m₀ at 10 % Mg), which helps carrier mobility.

### 2.2 Ti‑induced narrowing / indirectness

- **First‑principles DFT+U** (U ≈ 3–4 eV for Ti‑3d) shows a Ti‑derived narrow band lying 0.2–0.4 eV below the Zn‑derived CBM. With increasing Ti concentration, these bands broaden and overlap, pulling the CBM down.
- **Band‑structure mapping** (angle‑resolved photoelectron spectroscopy, ARPES) on Ti‑doped ZnO thin films finds a **Γ‑M crossing** where the CBM shifts from Γ to a point along Γ‑M, evidencing an indirect gap when x > 0.03.
- **Hybrid functional (HSE06)** predicts the indirect transition energy to be ~0.1–0.2 eV lower than the direct one, consistent with observed red‑shift of the absorption edge.

---

## 3. Electrical properties

| Property | Mg‑doped ZnO | Ti‑doped ZnO |
|----------|--------------|--------------|
| **Carrier type** | Typically **n‑type** (native), but Mg does not add carriers; can become semi‑insulating if V_O suppressed. | Strong **n‑type** (donor density ≈ 10¹⁸‑10²⁰ cm⁻³) due to Ti⁴⁺ → 2 e⁻ per Ti. |
| **Resistivity** | Increases with Mg (up to 10⁴ Ω·cm for 30 % Mg, unless co‑doped). | Decreases dramatically (down to 10⁻³ Ω·cm) even for x ~ 0.01. |
| **Mobility** | Slightly **enhanced** (up to 40 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹) for low Mg because of reduced ionized‑impurity scattering; deteriorates above ≈ 20 % Mg due to alloy scattering. | **Reduced** (10‑20 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹) because of ionized‑impurity and polaron scattering; at very high Ti, mobility may drop < 5 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. |
| **Temperature dependence** | Metallic‑like (weakly decreasing ρ with T) if background donors dominate; activated behaviour if Mg suppresses donors. | Typically **degenerate** (ρ ≈ constant) once Ti concentration > 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, but a **thermally‑activated hopping** component appears at low T (< 100 K) due to Ti‑related polarons. |

### 3.1 Defect chemistry equations (Kroger–Vink notation)

- **Mg**:  
  \[
  \text{MgO} \rightarrow \text{Mg}_{\text{Zn}}^{\prime} + V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  (Mg²⁺ is isovalent, so the reaction is *neutral*; the real effect is the **suppression** of \(V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet}\) because the lattice is tighter).

- **Ti**:  
  \[
  \text{TiO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  or, more commonly, direct donation:  
  \[
  \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\bullet\bullet} \rightarrow \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\times} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  where \( \bullet \) denotes a +1 effective charge relative to the lattice site.

---

## 4. Optical properties

| Property | Mg‑doped ZnO | Ti‑doped ZnO |
|----------|--------------|--------------|
| **Absorption edge** | Shifts to **shorter wavelength** (UV) – e.g., 380 nm → 340 nm for 15 % Mg. | Shifts to **longer wavelength** (visible) – “tail” extending to 500‑700 nm for > 2 % Ti. |
| **Exciton peak** | Remains sharp (~3.37 eV) but moves with band edge; linewidth may narrow due to reduced disorder. | Broadening and reduction of the excitonic peak; sometimes completely quenched for x > 0.02. |
| **Photoluminescence (PL)** | Near‑band‑edge (NBE) emission moves to higher energy; deep‑level green‑orange emission is suppressed. | Strong **deep‑level emission** (green/yellow) due to Ti‑related oxygen‑vacancy complexes; NBE intensity drops. |
| **Refractive index (n)** | Increases modestly (Δn ≈ +0.02 at 500 nm for 10 % Mg) because the band gap moves away from the wavelength. | Slight **decrease** (Δn ≈ ‑0.01) and strong dispersion near the Ti‑induced sub‑gap absorption. |
| **Non‑linear/transparent window** | Wider UV transparent window → useful for **deep‑UV photodetectors** or **transparent electrodes** at λ < 370 nm. | Additional absorption in the visible reduces transparency, but the high carrier density makes Ti‑ZnO attractive for **plasmonic** applications (e.g., ENZ at near‑IR). |

### 4.1 Mechanistic origins of the optical changes

1. **Band‑gap shift** (Burstein‑Moss effect) is **minor** at low carrier densities; the dominant shift for Mg is the **intrinsic CB rise**. For Ti, the shift is partly *opposite* (band‑gap narrowing) and partly **band‑tailing** (Urbach tail) caused by disorder/defect states.

2. **Urbach energy (E_U)** – a measure of disorder – grows from ~30 meV (pure ZnO) to ~80 meV (5 % Ti) but *decreases* to ~20 meV for 20 % Mg, reflecting the higher structural order of the Mg‑alloyed lattice.

3. **Free‑carrier absorption** – the Drude term – becomes appreciable for Ti‑ZnO (plasmonic response at λ ≈ 1–2 µm) while it is negligible for Mg‑ZnO unless the film is heavily co‑doped.

---

## 5. Underlying physical mechanisms – a concise “cause‑and‑effect” map

1. **Ionic size mismatch → strain → altered Zn–O bond lengths → modified crystal‑field splitting**  
   - Mg: compressive → larger s‑p overlap → higher CBM.  
   - Ti: local relaxation + high charge → mixed strain → d‑level hybridisation.

2. **Valence‑difference (charge) → defect formation**  
   - Isovalent Mg → *suppression* of intrinsic donors, higher resistivity.  
   - Heterovalent Ti⁴⁺ → *donor* generation, oxygen vacancies, high n‑type carrier density.

3. **Electronic configuration (s vs d) → band‑edge composition**  
   - Mg contributes empty 3s (high‑energy) → widens gap.  
   - Ti contributes partially filled 3d → creates localized states and can pull the CB down / make it indirect.

4. **Polaron formation (electron‑lattice coupling) → mobility & sub‑gap absorption**  
   - Ti‑3d electrons are prone to small‑polaron formation → hopping conduction, IR absorption.  
   - Mg lacks d‑electrons → negligible polaronic effects.

5. **Alloy disorder → Urbach tail & indirectness**  
   - Random distribution of Mg/Ti creates potential fluctuations; the stronger the fluctuation (Ti > 2 %), the larger the tail and the more likely an indirect transition becomes.

---

## 6. Practical implications

| Application | Preferred dopant | Reason |
|-------------|------------------|--------|
| **Transparent conductive oxide (TCO)** | **Mg** (often co‑doped with Al or Ga) | Wide band gap → high transparency; low free‑carrier absorption if co‑doped appropriately; resistivity can be tuned. |
| **UV photodetector / solar‑blind devices** | **Mg** (≥ 20 % for band gap > 4 eV) | Moves cutoff to deep‑UV, suppresses visible response. |
| **Highly conductive ZnO (e.g., electrodes, plasmonics)** | **Ti** (≤ 5 % to avoid secondary phases) | Very high n‑type carrier concentration; Drude response useful for ENZ and plasmonic metasurfaces. |
| **Spin‑tronic / dilute‑magnetic semiconductor** | **Ti** (if Ti³⁺ present) | Ti³⁺ (d¹) can introduce magnetic moments; however, magnetic ordering is still debated. |
| **Band‑gap engineering for LEDs** | **Mg + Ti** (gradient/combinatorial) | Mg sets the high‑energy edge; Ti introduces deep states that can serve as recombination centers for visible emission. |

---

## 7. Key literature and modelling tools (for quick reference)

| Topic | Representative papers / reviews | Modeling approaches |
|------|----------------------------------|---------------------|
| Mg‑ZnO alloy | *Kuznetsov et al., J. Appl. Phys. 2020*; *Khan et al., Adv. Funct. Mater. 2022* | Vegard’s law + DFT‑GGA; hybrid functional band‑gap calculations |
| Ti‑doped ZnO | *Kim et al., Phys. Rev. B 2019*; *Li & Zhang, Appl. Phys. Lett. 2021* | DFT+U (U ≈ 3 eV); GW for accurate CBM positioning |
| Defect chemistry | *Look, *Semiconductors and Semimetals* vol 84 (2012)* | Kroger‑Vink formalism + first‑principles defect formation energies |
| Optical constants | *Mong et al., Optics Express 2023* (spectroscopic ellipsometry) | Drude‑Lorentz fitting; Tauc‑Plot analysis with Urbach tail |
| Polaron transport | *Mancini et al., J. Phys. Chem. C 2020* | Small‑polaron hopping models (Marcus theory) + temperature‑dependent conductivity |

---

### Bottom line

- **Mg** acts mostly as a **size‑matching, isovalent, s‑type alloying element** that **compresses the lattice**, **pushes the conduction band up**, **keeps the gap direct**, and **improves transparency** while reducing intrinsic donor concentration.  
- **Ti** is a **high‑valent, d‑electron dopant** that **creates donor electrons**, **introduces Ti‑3d impurity bands**, can **make the gap indirect or create deep sub‑gap states**, **increases free‑carrier absorption**, and **induces polaronic hopping**.  

Understanding which mechanism dominates at a given concentration lets you tailor ZnO for anything from **UV‑transparent electrodes** (Mg‑rich) to **high‑conductivity plasmonic layers** (Ti‑rich), or to engineer intermediate band structures for **photovoltaic up‑conversion** by mixing both dopants in a controlled gradient.

| **Carrier type** | Typically **n‑type** (native), but Mg does not add carriers; can become semi‑insulating if V_O suppressed. | Strong **n‑type** (donor density ≈ 10¹⁸‑10²⁰ cm⁻³) due to Ti⁴⁺ → 2 e⁻ per Ti. |
| **Resistivity** | Increases with Mg (up to 10⁴ Ω·cm for 30 % Mg, unless co‑doped). | Decreases dramatically (down to 10⁻³ Ω·cm) even for x ~ 0.01. |
| **Mobility** | Slightly **enhanced** (up to 40 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹) for low Mg because of reduced ionized‑impurity scattering; deteriorates above ≈ 20 % Mg due to alloy scattering. | **Reduced** (10‑20 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹) because of ionized‑impurity and polaron scattering; at very high Ti, mobility may drop < 5 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. |
| **Temperature dependence** | Metallic‑like (weakly decreasing ρ with T) if background donors dominate; activated behaviour if Mg suppresses donors. | Typically **degenerate** (ρ ≈ constant) once Ti concentration > 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, but a **thermally‑activated hopping** component appears at low T (< 100 K) due to Ti‑related polarons. |

### 3.1 Defect chemistry equations (Kroger–Vink notation)

- **Mg**:  
  \[
  \text{MgO} \rightarrow \text{Mg}_{\text{Zn}}^{\prime} + V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  (Mg²⁺ is isovalent, so the reaction is *neutral*; the real effect is the **suppression** of \(V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet}\) because the lattice is tighter).

- **Ti**:  
  \[
  \text{TiO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2V_{\text{O}}^{\bullet\bullet} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  or, more commonly, direct donation:  
  \[
  \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\bullet\bullet} \rightarrow \text{Ti}_{\text{Zn}}^{\times} + 2e^{-}
  \]  
  where \( \bullet \) denotes a +1 effective charge relative to the lattice site.

---

## 4. Optical properties

| Property | Mg‑doped ZnO | Ti‑doped ZnO |
|----------|--------------|--------------|
| **Absorption edge** | Shifts to **shorter wavelength** (UV) – e.g., 380 nm → 340 nm for 15 % Mg. | Shifts to **longer wavelength** (visible) – “tail” extending to 500‑700 nm for > 2 % Ti. |
| **Exciton peak** | Remains sharp (~3.37 eV) but moves with band edge; linewidth may narrow due to reduced disorder. | Broadening and reduction of the excitonic peak; sometimes completely quenched for x > 0.02. |
| **Photoluminescence (PL)** | Near‑band‑edge (NBE) emission moves to higher energy; deep‑level green‑orange emission is suppressed. | Strong **deep‑level emission** (green/yellow) due to Ti‑related oxygen‑vacancy complexes; NBE intensity drops. |
| **Refractive index (n)** | Increases modestly (Δn ≈ +0.02 at 500 nm for 10 % Mg) because the band gap moves away from the wavelength. | Slight **decrease** (Δn ≈ ‑0.01) and strong dispersion near the Ti‑induced sub‑gap absorption. |
| **Non‑linear/transparent window** | Wider UV transparent window → useful for **deep‑UV photodetectors** or **transparent electrodes** at λ < 370 nm. | Additional absorption in the visible reduces transparency, but the high carrier density makes Ti‑ZnO attractive for **plasmonic** applications (e.g., ENZ at near‑IR). |

### 4.1 Mechanistic origins of the optical changes

1. **Band‑gap shift** (Burstein‑Moss effect) is **minor** at low carrier densities; the dominant shift for Mg is the **intrinsic CB rise**. For Ti, the shift is partly *opposite* (band‑gap narrowing) and partly **band‑tailing** (Urbach tail) caused by disorder/defect states.

2. **Urbach energy (E_U)** – a measure of disorder – grows from ~30 meV (pure ZnO) to ~80 meV (5 % Ti) but *decreases* to ~20 meV for 20 % Mg, reflecting the higher structural order of the Mg‑alloyed lattice.

3. **Free‑carrier absorption** – the Drude term – becomes appreciable for Ti‑ZnO (plasmonic response at λ ≈ 1–2 µm) while it is negligible for Mg‑ZnO unless the film is heavily co‑doped.

---

## 5. Underlying physical mechanisms – a concise “cause‑and‑effect” map

1. **Ionic size mismatch → strain → altered Zn–O bond lengths → modified crystal‑field splitting**  
   - Mg: compressive → larger s‑p overlap → higher CBM.  
   - Ti: local relaxation + high charge → mixed strain → d‑level hybridisation.

2. **Valence‑difference (charge) → defect formation**  
   - Isovalent Mg → *suppression* of intrinsic donors, higher resistivity.  
   - Heterovalent Ti⁴⁺ → *donor* generation, oxygen vacancies, high n‑type carrier density.

3. **Electronic configuration (s vs d) → band‑edge composition**  
   - Mg contributes empty 3s (high‑energy) → widens gap.  
   - Ti contributes partially filled 3d → creates localized states and can pull the CB down / make it indirect.

4. **Polaron formation (electron‑lattice coupling) → mobility & sub‑gap absorption**  
   - Ti‑3d electrons are prone to small‑polaron formation → hopping conduction, IR absorption.  
   - Mg lacks d‑electrons → negligible polaronic effects.

5. **Alloy disorder → Urbach tail & indirectness**  
   - Random distribution of Mg/Ti creates potential fluctuations; the stronger the fluctuation (Ti > 2 %), the larger the tail and the more likely an indirect transition becomes.

---

## 6. Practical implications

| Application | Preferred dopant | Reason |
|-------------|------------------|--------|
| **Transparent conductive oxide (TCO)** | **Mg** (often co‑doped with Al or Ga) | Wide band gap → high transparency; low free‑carrier absorption if co‑doped appropriately; resistivity can be tuned. |
| **UV photodetector / solar‑blind devices** | **Mg** (≥ 20 % for band gap > 4 eV) | Moves cutoff to deep‑UV, suppresses visible response. |
| **Highly conductive ZnO (e.g., electrodes, plasmonics)** | **Ti** (≤ 5 % to avoid secondary phases) | Very high n‑type carrier concentration; Drude response useful for ENZ and plasmonic metasurfaces. |
| **Spin‑tronic / dilute‑magnetic semiconductor** | **Ti** (if Ti³⁺ present) | Ti³⁺ (d¹) can introduce magnetic moments; however, magnetic ordering is still debated. |
| **Band‑gap engineering for LEDs** | **Mg + Ti** (gradient/combinatorial) | Mg sets the high‑energy edge; Ti introduces deep states that can serve as recombination centers for visible emission. |

---

## 7. Key literature and modelling tools (for quick reference)

| Topic | Representative papers / reviews | Modeling approaches |
|------|----------------------------------|---------------------|
| Mg‑ZnO alloy | *Kuznetsov et al., J. Appl. Phys. 2020*; *Khan et al., Adv. Funct. Mater. 2022* | Vegard’s law + DFT‑GGA; hybrid functional band‑gap calculations |
| Ti‑doped ZnO | *Kim et al., Phys. Rev. B 2019*; *Li & Zhang, Appl. Phys. Lett. 2021* | DFT+U (U ≈ 3 eV); GW for accurate CBM positioning |
| Defect chemistry | *Look, *Semiconductors and Semimetals* vol 84 (2012)* | Kroger‑Vink formalism + first‑principles defect formation energies |
| Optical constants | *Mong et al., Optics Express 2023* (spectroscopic ellipsometry) | Drude‑Lorentz fitting; Tauc‑Plot analysis with Urbach tail |
| Polaron transport | *Mancini et al., J. Phys. Chem. C 2020* | Small‑polaron hopping models (Marcus theory) + temperature‑dependent conductivity |

---

### Bottom line

- **Mg** acts mostly as a **size‑matching, isovalent, s‑type alloying element** that **compresses the lattice**, **pushes the conduction band up**, **keeps the gap direct**, and **improves transparency** while reducing intrinsic donor concentration.  
- **Ti** is a **high‑valent, d‑electron dopant** that **creates donor electrons**, **introduces Ti‑3d impurity bands**, can **make the gap indirect or create deep sub‑gap states**, **increases free‑carrier absorption**, and **induces polaronic hopping**.  

Understanding which mechanism dominates at a given concentration lets you tailor ZnO for anything from **UV‑transparent electrodes** (Mg‑rich) to **high‑conductivity plasmonic layers** (Ti‑rich), or to engineer intermediate band structures for **photovoltaic up‑conversion** by mixing both dopants in a controlled gradient.

final state is a pair of light leptons | The SM amplitude is proportional to \(\displaystyle \frac{m_\ell}{M_{B}}\) (from the V–A structure of the weak interaction). For muons this gives a factor \(\sim 0.03\). | A scalar or pseudoscalar operator (e.g. from a Higgs‑like boson) is not helicity‑suppressed, so its contribution can be orders of magnitude larger than the SM one for the same coupling strength. | | **CKM suppression**
proportional to \(|V_{tb}V_{ts}^*|\) (for \(B_s\)) or \(|V_{tb}V_{td}^*|\) (for \(B_d\)) | Values \(\sim 4\times10^{-2}\) and \(\sim 8\times10^{-3}\), respectively, make the SM rate tiny. | NP models often introduce new flavour‑changing couplings that are not tied to the CKM hierarchy, so they can lift the suppression. | | **Clean theoretical environment**

The SM branching fractions (including the latest lattice inputs for \(f_{B_q}\) and the CKM elements) are \[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm SM} &= (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9},\\[4pt] \mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm SM} &= (1.06\pm0.09)\times10^{-10}. \end{aligned}} \] The quoted uncertainties are dominated by the CKM factors (\(\sim 4\%\)) and the decay constants (\(\sim 2\%\)). The numbers assume the current world‑average (combined LHCb‑CMS‑ATLAS) \[ \mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm exp}= (2.99\pm0.31)\times10^{-9}, \qquad \mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm exp}= (1.5^{+1.2}_{-1.0})\times10^{-10}, \] which are compatible with the SM at the 1–2 σ level. | Model | Typical NP contribution to the effective Hamiltonian | Translating the measured \(\mathcal{B}\) into a bound | |-------|------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------| | **Minimal Supersymmetric SM (MSSM) with large \(\tan\beta\)** | Dominant scalar/pseudoscalar Higgs exchange → \[C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}\simeq -\frac{( \tan\beta)^3 }{M_A^2}\,\frac{Y_t^2\,\mu A_t}{16\pi^2}\] (proportional to \(\tan^3\beta\) and inversely to the CP‑odd Higgs mass \(M_A\)). | The measured \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) forces \(\displaystyle \frac{\tan\beta}{M_A}\lesssim 0.04\;{\rm GeV}^{-1}\). For \(\tan\beta=50\) one needs \(M_A\gtrsim 1.2\;{\rm TeV}\). | | **Z′ boson with flavour‑changing coupling \(g_{bs}\)** | Tree‑level contribution to the vector operator: \[C_{10}^{\rm NP}= \frac{g_{bs}\,g_{\ell\ell}}{M_{Z'}^2}\] | The bound \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.07\) (≈ 2 % of the SM \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\)) translates into \(\displaystyle \frac{g_{bs} g_{\ell\ell}}{M_{Z'}^2}\lesssim 1.5\times 10^{-9}\;{\rm GeV}^{-2}\). Typically \[C_{10}^{\rm NP}\simeq -\frac{v^2}{2M_{U_1}^2}\, \lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}^\ast\] | Using the experimental limit, \(|\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}^\ast|/M_{U_1}^2\lesssim 1.0\times10^{-9}\,{\rm GeV}^{-2}\). For \(\lambda\sim1\) the leptoquark must be heavier than \(\sim 30\) TeV, far beyond current direct‑search reach, unless the couplings are hierarchical. | | **Effective field theory (SMEFT) dimension‑6 operators** | Operators such as \((\phi^\dagger i\!\!\overleftrightarrow{D}_\mu\phi)(\bar q \gamma^\mu P_L b)\) map onto \(C_{10}\) after electroweak symmetry breaking. The Wilson coefficient at the weak scale \(\tilde C_{lq}^{(1)}\) contributes as \(\displaystyle C_{10}^{\rm NP}= \frac{v^2}{\Lambda^2}\tilde C_{lq}^{(1)}\). | The limit \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim0.07\) gives \(\displaystyle \Lambda/\sqrt{|\tilde C_{lq}^{(1)}|}\gtrsim 5\ {\rm TeV}\). If the operator coefficient is \(\mathcal O(1)\), new physics must lie above ∼ 5 TeV. | *The numbers above are illustrative; precise limits depend on the assumed spectrum (e.g. masses of SUSY particles) and on whether other flavour observables are simultaneously fitted.* --- ### 5. Why the **ratio** \(\displaystyle R_{\mu\mu}\equiv\frac{\mathcal{B}(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)}\) is an extra powerful handle * In the SM the ratio is essentially \[ R_{\mu\mu}^{\rm SM}= \frac{\tau_{B_d}}{\tau_{B_s}}\, \frac{M_{B_d}}{M_{B_s}}\, \left(\frac{f_{B_d}}{f_{B_s}}\right)^2 \left|\frac{V_{td}}{V_{ts}}\right|^2 \simeq 0.029\pm0.003 . \] The CKM factor \(|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\) is the dominant source of uncertainty (≈ 10 %); all other hadronic inputs are known to sub‑percent precision. * Many NP models affect **both** decays in a correlated way (e.g. a heavy Z′ that couples universally to down‑type quarks). In many concrete models this will push the viable mass scale for flavor‑changing mediators beyond the direct‑search reach, turning the rare‑decay measurements into the **most stringent indirect bound**. --- ### 7. Take‑away summary 1. **FCNC + helicity suppression = tiny SM rate.** This makes any additional short‑distance contribution proportionally large. 2. **Theoretical cleanliness.** Only the decay constant \(f_{B_q}\) enters, known to a few percent, so the SM prediction is precise. 3. **Branching fractions map directly onto Wilson coefficients** \(C_{10},C_{S},C_{P}\). In short, the rare decays \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\) and \(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-\) are *precision microscopes* that turn the tiny SM prediction into a lever‑arm for testing, and potentially falsifying, many extensions of the Standard Model.

question: How do precise measurements of rare neutral B meson decays into muon pairs constrain extensions of the Standard Model, and which classes of new-physics models are most strongly affected by these results?

### 1. Any new heavy particle that couples to quarks or leptons can enter the same loops and change the amplitude. | Combined LHCb + CMS measurement (Run‑2 + Run‑3 data) gives
\(\mathcal{B}(B_s^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-) = (3.09 \pm 0.16_{\rm stat}\pm0.06_{\rm syst})\times10^{-9}\)
\(\mathcal{B}(B_d^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-) = (1.01 \pm 0.24_{\rm stat}\pm0.07_{\rm syst})\times10^{-10}\)
Both compatible with the SM at the 5 % level. | | **Helicity suppression** | The SM amplitude is proportional to the muon mass, \(\propto m_\mu\), because a pseudoscalar → lepton‑pair transition requires a chirality flip. A global fit therefore tightly correlates all these modes. | Global fits (e.g. “flavio 2.5”, “EOS”) show that any NP contribution to \(C_{10}\) must be ≲ 5 % of the SM value, while scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients are bound at the \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})\) level. | Because **the SM prediction is razor‑sharp and the measurement now matches it within uncertainties**, any deviation must be small. The **branching ratio** can be written (to excellent accuracy) as \[ \mathcal{B}(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-) = \underbrace{\frac{G_F^2\alpha^2}{16\pi^3} \, \tau_{B_q} M_{B_q} f_{B_q}^2 |V_{tb}V_{tq}^\ast|^2}_{\displaystyle \text{SM normalisation}} \sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{M_{B_q}^2}} \Bigl[|S|^2\Bigl(1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{M_{B_q}^2}\Bigr) + |P|^2\Bigr], \] with \[ \begin{aligned} P &= C_{10}^{\rm SM} + C_{10}^{\rm NP} - \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2m_\mu(m_b+m_q)}(C_{P}^{\rm NP}-C_{P}^{\prime\rm NP}),\\ S &= \sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{M_{B_q}^2}} \,\frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2m_\mu(m_b+m_q)}(C_{S}^{\rm NP}-C_{S}^{\prime\rm NP}) . \end{aligned} \] Since the measured rates are SM‑like, **\(S\) must be tiny** (scalar/pseudoscalar NP ≲ 10 % of the SM amplitude) and **\(P\) can deviate from its SM value by at most a few percent**. This reduces the viable parameter space dramatically and is usually displayed as exclusion contours in the \((M,\;g)\) plane. 3. **Future projections**: The upgraded LHCb (Run‑4 and Run‑5) aims for a **~5 % total uncertainty** on \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu\mu)\) and the first observation of the time‑dependent CP asymmetry (sensitive to the phase of \(C_{10}\)). A further improvement to **~2 %** (possible with a high‑luminosity flavour factory) would push the limits on scalar coefficients down to the **\(10^{-4}\)** level, essentially closing the window on any NP that does not decouple at > 10 TeV. --- ### 4.
